items.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
items.author: QueensGambit
items.content:
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:

  1. First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation.
  2. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID.
  3. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.
All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.

What is the right code for this?

If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:
  1. Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone.
  2. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.
In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack.
AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.
Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.

Your new job is to architect

AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:
  1. Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app.
  2. Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.
That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.
If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.

items.title: Vibecoding an inference chip
items.author: ankitvgupta
items.content:
One of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely new domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms. Lately, that has meant hacking on hardware, now that writing low-level software is much easier. So, in this blog post, I’m going to try to recount the experience of vibe coding an FPGA, going through a series of “oh shit” moments several times, and giving myself a new appreciation for what’s possible if you have a large token budget (thanks YC) and interesting problems to point the models at.

I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work. I’ll admit I was relatively naive about them. I’d never really experimented with them in my startup or in college, so I knew little about them before. The basic idea I was familiar with: you can program a circuit into a reprogrammable chip. So rather than having a general purpose computing architecture (like a CPU) you can have a reprogrammable one, i.e. the configuration loaded onto the chip determines how its logic and routing are connected, and that (in theory) enables performance advantages. I also know that it took a mountain of C++ to write and involved manually analyzing waveforms for simulation and verification. I had never done this before though and it seemed cumbersome.

That’s about what I knew going into this.

Naturally, my ML brain thought “could we use these for AI inference”. I’m not the first to think this — there are a few repos attempting to port ML models to FPGAs on Github. But I hadn’t actually seen a writeup on whether coding agents are good at writing the low level C++ and Verilog code to program them and verifying the outputs so that they actually run accurately. (Spoiler alert, they are incredible at programming them.)

So I decided I needed to get my hands on one. AWS has F2 instances with FPGA hardware, and that seemed easier than going and buying physical hardware, so I asked Codex to spin up a reservation and got cooking. It had a relatively limited memory of 16 GB of FPGA HBM. Around the same time, I was working with the DeepGrove founders who were discussing their new ternary weight architecture that is well suited for memory limited cases. It’s SOTA on Mac hardware with actual agentic tool calling, so I figured why not, let’s see if I can get this working on an FPGA and fast enough to be useful.

What followed was a cloud agent running in Conductor for several days with me mostly just encouraging it periodically while it both (1) got a model fully running and (2) increased its speed by 33× from the first full-model bit-exact baseline to get it to a real-time relevant speed. It was one of the most mind blowing autoresearch loops I’ve run, ultimately writing roughly 3M lines across the experiment history and parsing 30M lines of output files, burning only $10,000 in Claude and OpenAI tokens to run hundreds of experiments. Most of the code is C++ and some Verilog. It’s been probably a decade since the last time I wrote any serious amount of C++ and I’ve never written Verilog. I honestly don’t know the first thing about Verilog. Most of my prompts were not particularly clever: they consisted mostly of me saying things like “you’re a superintelligent model, time to be more creative” and “let’s go for 2x faster, you got this”. Sometimes I brought some ML knowhow like “hey it’s time to consider speculative decoding” or “why is that running on CPU, you should port it”. But for the most part, it was just vibes and I’m pretty sure that with enough time the model would have figured out those things. Also, it seemed that both Astra and Opus (new Fable wasn’t out yet) were pretty capable at this and I could use them interchangeably. I’m sure someone has a good benchmark for which is smarter but both passed my smart-enough threshold.

From “it works” to 213 tokens per second

The chart follows the measured optimization sequence: , or the baseline.

How much did the human advice help?

At one point, around when it got to 10 TPS, I messaged the DeepGrove founders about this, and they replied surprised that it was working so easily, saying they had tried this a few months back and the models were not quite good enough to be particularly effective. They sent me a prompt that summarizes some of their lessons and I copy-pasted it into my session to see if it’d matter. It was essentially the most significant piece of actual guidance I added to this session. The prompt is reproduced below.

The coding agent diligently considered these asks, but it didn’t seem to make all that much of a difference qualitatively. Indeed, when I asked it later to read all of the logs and determine which of these instructions it actually used, it said:

In other words, for most of the actual design ideas it is unclear but there is good reason to believe the model would have figured them out, especially because it came up with them many cycles later after several compaction cycles. But the process advice was useful immediately for getting to hardware results sooner and increasing iteration speed. In other words, the humans are still useful at defining how to iterate fast and what correctness looks like, and the agents are great to manage the exploration.

Here are the changes the autoresearch loop found. Interestingly, it’s mostly a series of modest improvements that compound 1.5x ish every time, rather than one or two giant ones.

It’s difficult to do a 1:1 comparison across these configurations. I didn’t run the same autoresearch loop on every alternative, and I assume there is more performance to extract if I did. The point is to show how slow the FPGA was in its first implementation, and how far the optimization loop took it.

The measurements below are from November 15 on AWS, replaying the same 8-chat × 3-turn benchmark. Prices are the on-demand rates recorded with that experiment. “Exact turns” counts outputs that matched the pinned CPU reference. The GPU implementations are included for context but did not satisfy the same bit-exact criterion but are pretty close in practice.

What happens as the context grows?

This is one generation starting with a 16-token prompt and continuing until the 8,192-token context is full: . The five middle columns show decode speed in at the indicated context length for several generations of iteration. The last column is wall-clock time for the whole run/

* For r8 and r9, the first two columns come from separate, shorter runs generating 2,032 tokens. The other columns come from the full-context run.

r9 improves short-context speed, while the complete long-context run is roughly tied with r8.

What the model actually says

These examples come from the final r9 image.

Arithmetic, with the steps

System prompt: “You are a helpful assistant. Think briefly before you answer, then reply clearly and concisely.”

This was a fun project. I’m not sure I’m ever going to use this specific chip architecture in this specific way, and I’m certainly not claiming that an 8,192-token-context model running on an FPGA is the way I’d recommend anyone use something like this in production. But it’s pretty epic that this . Capability like this completely shifts the overton window for what a committed team of engineers can work on. It should mean that entirely new types of ideas (scientific discoveries, products, startups) are possible if you can point the models in the right direction. I’m excited to see what everyone builds.

items.title: Google Workers Tell Their Employer Not to Punish Schools That Don't Want AI
items.author: cdrnsf
items.content:
Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free .

at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the company’s search engine starting next year.

Google made the surprise announcement two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom. Since then, communities across the country have protested Google’s tight hold on tech in many schools.

Attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.

Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on.

That day, protests took place in six other cities—Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations.

School districts across the country use the company’s software and Chromebooks, which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search embeds AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini. 

Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US—New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago—are now discussing alternative search engines. 

“Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum,” employees wrote in a petition brought by the Alphabet Workers Union, which represents more than 1,000 workers at Google’s parent company. “Cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether.”

“It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products,” they continued, addressing Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Reid, its vice president and head of search.

A software engineer in Google’s education department told me on Thursday that most workers did not know about the Google Search decision before it was publicly announced. Corporate leadership has now acknowledged the letter but has not responded to any of itsspecific demands. 

AI classroom tools should be “built responsibly and prioritize the best interests of the students, not the company’s bottom line,” the Google engineer said.

Another engineer and union member in New York, who also signed the petition, said to that the executive team “seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision.”

That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students: the Google staffer said their colleagues are also concerned about how the company is implementing their work on AI tools.

“If the tech is really as useful and desirable as they think it is, why don’t they trust us to choose to use it on our own terms?” the engineer asked.

Google has been contacted for comment.

items.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day
items.author: cdrnsf
items.content:
As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

items.title: The Making of Oxygene
items.author: hggh
items.content:
In late 1976, an album was released which re-wrote the rulebook of synthesizers and electronic music and captured the hearts and imagination of the entire world. Composed by the then unknown 28-year-old French artist Jean-Michel Jarre, the album Oxygène broke out of France to become a top 10 album in seven different countries, spending a remarkable 24 weeks in the UK album charts and selling now close to 20 million copies worldwide.

Uniquely, the album consisted of just six tracks, numbered Oxygène Parts 1 through 6, and was entirely instrumental with no acoustic instruments whatsoever, which was unheard of in 1976.

Jean Michel Jarre tells the story of the making of his ground-breaking album in his own words.

"Around 1969, I felt that the world of classical music, the world of rock and other forms of music were a bit narrow and living in their own worlds. I had the feeling it was the right time to explore other fields to perhaps see if a combination of different styles were possible.

“The main difference with electronic music is that you create music in terms of sound, not just notes. It’s something else entirely. When I was a teenager, I always liked processing my guitar or organ or whatever, playing the tape backwards and changing the speed. Then the drummer in my band said, ‘You should meet with these crazy guys at Groupe De Recherches Musicales [GRM] in Paris who are working in French public radio. They’re doing the same kinds of things as you, and they have labs.’

“When I first went there, I was immediately seduced by what they were doing. Electronic music owes a lot to public radio stations - the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, the German lab where Stockhausen was working and, of course, the one in Paris.

"Pierre Schaeffer was one of the most brilliant guys of the century in terms of what he brought to the music world. He created the notion of Musique concrète and influenced me a lot in this direction. Saying that, I felt that contemporary music had got a very elitist attitude - a bit too intellectual vis-à-vis the music and it created barriers between the audience and yourself. I wanted to be much more open to the audience.

"I stayed with Pierre Schaeffer [and Pierre Henry] for three years and I also went to Cologne to work with Stockhausen. He was totally crazy, but a real genius. He considered himself to be made of sound, biologically, so he had a kind of surrealistic approach. Crazy, but realistic at the same time. It was very interesting.

"When I left GRM and through to 1976, I did production work for some rock artists, earning enough to set up a studio in my kitchen. I didn’t have much equipment, though, just a few guitar pedals and my first synthesizer, the VCS3, which looked like a telephone exchange. I realised that using a Revox tape machine to delay the sound that came out of one loudspeaker created a huge sense of space.

“The British-made VCS3 from EMS [Electronic Music Studios, based in London] was created by a genius called Peter Zinovieff. It was a kind of poor European version of the Moog. In those days Europe was not as rich as the States, so the sound was drier. In a sense, it was a kind of punk synthesizer - there was something very harsh and rough about it. I loved it; I still take one on stage with me today.

“At the time, I was obsessed with this idea of creating a bridge between experimentation and pop melody. I liked this kind of challenge, playing around with sound design and integrating melodies. Oxygène was a new start for music with analogue synthesizers"

The album was recorded on a Scully recorder with just eight tracks, and all through a home-made mixer. On top of the VCS3, Jarre had managed to add some other classic equipment including EMS Synthi AKS and ARP 2600 synths, an Eminent String Ensemble, an RMI Harmonic Synthesizer, and Farfisa organ, while an RMI Keyboard Computer was used for some sequencing.

Jarre continues, “I really did it in a kind of home way using what, I think, was one of the first home studios. I had just three or four synthesizers and was using a Scully eight–track and a mixture of Ampex 256 and 3M tape. The whole album was done on just one eight–track and you can hear that in the piece — it’s quite minimalist and I think that contributes to its timelessness.

“Nothing is repeated the same way. Each sound, even if appears to be the same, has a slightly different attack and release, and, as the sequences are being made by hand, by definition they are not the same. Even the sounds of the drum machines were filtered in a very subtle way to give life inside the patterns.

”Michel Geiss was a maintenance technician, at a famous French record company at that time called Barclay and I met him because he was very interested in electronic instruments. He visited my home and we started to experiment. He was teaching me to use the first semi-modular synths I could put my hands on. And then step by step we worked together, Michel mainly as a kind of sound engineer for me.

“For Oxygene, he was working at his record company as a maintenance guy during the day, and he was coming to work with me at night. In those days I probably had the first home studio in France, when the serious music was done in serious recording studios with a window where God was the sound engineer behind the window, and we were just on the other side as musicians. For electronic music you need to match the mixing area with the main studio to record your own sounds.

“So, I had this home studio in a kitchen in the flat I had in Paris, and Michel joined me, using one of the first eight-track tape recorders to record my music. I only had two tapes. So, I had no choice if I was not happy with something to erase what I'd done the previous day, and this is the reason why I have no archive of material from Oxygène. It's such a shame.

“And that is also the reason why if you take the master tape of Oxygène, it is made up of two different tapes. Right in the middle of part one of Oxygène, I had one piece I really liked, where suddenly in the first part you have this kind of brassy, quite epic brassy moment. This is coming from another tape that I recorded another time.

“I thought to myself that it's really matching very well. So, I did a very strong edit, quite dramatic edit, by cutting the two tapes together, even the colours are different. One is pink, one is black. It's totally crazy. And whilst you can't hear the edit, it's quite challenging to cut an eight-track tape like this.

“With so little to work with, I had to be creative. My old Mellotron only had a few working keys, but I still managed to write Oxygene Part II on it. My primitive drum machine - a Korg Mini Pops was the sort of thing people played in pubs, but by using Sellotape I could make it play two preset rhythms at the same time, creating cool beats. Oxygène Part IV, which became iconic, was a mixture of [presets] Slow Rock and Rock, while Part VI combined Rumba and Bossa Nova.

“But when I finished the album, because Oxygène consisted of entirely instrumental music, none of the record companies thought it would work. The only people who took the risk were a small French company called Dreyfus Music. Even after it had become a hit in France, people said it couldn't possibly be a success anywhere else. Then eventually, after it got to the top of the charts in Britain and all over Europe, the critics explained that it was successful because of its originality and because of its use of melody. It's easy to be wise after the event!

“I made the first album back in the days of vinyl, when we were always thinking about sides one and two. The other characteristic of Oxygène is that it has sunny melodies but it’s also quite dark, like the cover artwork.”

Studio engineer and would-be long-time collaborator Michel Geiss, has fond memories of his first encounter with Jean Michel Jarre, recalling, "Oxygene marked the beginning of my collaboration with Jean-Michel. At the time, I was working during the day at a large studio complex in Paris called Studios Barclay. I was employed there as a technician. The recording studios were located on the upper floors, while I worked in the workshop downstairs. My body was downstairs, but my mind was upstairs! I felt strongly attracted to the world of music engineering, although I wasn't particularly interested in the equipment I had been assigned to work with.

"In fact, I found the right balance when I began working with Jean-Michel at his own studio around the same time. Every day, once my working day at Barclay had finished, I would join Jean-Michel in his studio, at his request, to work on his album. We would continue until I had to catch the last train home. I remember him calling me every afternoon to ask if I could come over.

"This was my first real opportunity to work in a studio as a sound and music collaborator, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. Jean-Michel would also occasionally ask for my musical opinion on various matters. I programmed some specific sounds on the ARP 2600, including the main theme sound in Oxygene IV and the sound of the waves in Part VI.

"It was a close working relationship, and I felt that I had finally found my rightful place. It suited me much better than simply being an electronics specialist, which was my background before I met him.

"My main role during the recording of Oxygene was to record Jean-Michel while he played his instruments, as he needed someone to handle the recording process.

"At the time, he was also keen to expand his relatively limited collection of instruments in order to explore new sounds. I suggested that we take a look at the RMI keyboards, which were sold in France by Piano Center in Montreuil. Jean-Michel immediately agreed, saying, 'OK, let's go!'

"When we arrived at the music shop, Jean-Michel discovered the two instruments I had suggested: the RMI Harmonic Synthesizer and the RMI Keyboard Computer. The latter used punched cardboard cards to store its sound information. The Harmonic Synthesizer had a truly distinctive sound and featured an arpeggiator. It would later prove to be a key instrument on the album, particularly on Oxygene IV."

The album’s iconic artwork came about when Jarre was visiting Marquet Gallery in Paris and a piece caught his eye that he was instantly drawn to. A painting of a skull hidden within the Earth. The painting was created by young artist Michel Granger, titled Oxygène. By chance, Granger happened to be in the gallery at the same time and the pair spoke and Jean-Michel bought the painting to use as the album cover and adopted its title.

Michel Granger recalls, “I was having my first major show in Paris. On display was a 30x40cm watercolour called Oxygène and Jean-Michel bought it, telling me he’d love to use it as an album cover. Oxygène was part of a series about the damage being done to our planet. It was quite a violent image for a record sleeve.

“The only change I made was to the background, making it square to fit the album shape. Jean-Michel and I chose the typography and that was that. We were both similar ages and he was very passionate about music and painting. We would have long conversations in the evenings, always at the same pizzeria, then he went home to compose all night.”

Jean Michel Jarre commented on the artwork,"What I like about this picture is that it isn’t necessarily pessimistic. It rather poses the question: where are we going?”

With its iconic title and cover set, and after the album was mixed at Studio Gang by Jean-Pierre Janiaud, an accomplished engineer, Jarre took the album to Francis Dreyfus, owner of the Disques Motors record label, who he had worked for during his songwriting days with Christophe. Dreyfus loved the album and was convinced it could be a success.

Dreyfus pressed 50,000 copies on his own label to sell in France and released the album in December 1976. Uniquely and a brainwave of Dreyfus and Jarre, they offered the album to nationwide hi-fi shops, given the album's innovative use of stereo. The idea being that high-end hi-fi buyers would buy a copy of the album to go with their hardware purchase. By April 1977, sales in France had reached 70,000 copies despite very little promotion. Legend has it that some people returned the LP believing the iconic white noise was a manufacturing defect. 

Finding an international label to distribute was harder. Initially no record company was interested in the album, citing no singer, no guitars, no drummer, no proper track titles, no obvious singles, and to round it off, it was French.

Everything changed when Fred Haayen, the new head of Polydor Records in London discovered the record in a French record store and signed it to the label.  He was instrumental in persuading BBC Radio 1 to play the album in full the week of release. The only other album to ever receive such an honour was Pink Floyd's Dark Side of the Moon. 

The album was mostly slated by the UK's mainstream music press, with the NME calling it “another interminable sonic cruise and infuriatingly derivative.” but the public loved the album and on August 23rd 1977, Oxygène entered the UK album charts at number 19, climbing and remaining in the top 10 for the next 11 weeks.  After moving to the United States to lead Polydor USA, Haayen also spearheaded the launch of the album in the US, to achieve official platinum status.

We’ll let Jarre conclude the story, “It’s now sold something like 18 million copies and, no matter what I do, I am defined by Oxygène. But that’s OK. It’s funny. At first, the album was played in hi-fi shops as an example of 'state-of-the-art sound'. I didn’t tell them I made it in my kitchen.

“When you’ve been lucky enough to have some kind of success with your first project, it will always be part of your DNA, no matter what you do afterwards. It’s like the first movie for Tarantino or Kubrick. For me, it’s the same with Oxygène. I love many other things that I’ve done and I’m very proud of them all, but Oxygène is something unique.”

items.title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
items.author: sammatilda
items.content:
Feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I said to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”

Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely.

I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with.

Feynman was also quoted as saying:

I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.

Pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read:

What I cannot create, I do not understand.

items.title: Restricting AI agents in mobile operating systems platforms from capturing data
items.author: dotcoma
items.content:
Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.

People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.

We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.

We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:

  1. Developers should have an easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing, including (but not limited to) screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, all without undermining the core utility of an application.
  2. Operating system companies should create better documentation and technical specifications around how these AI agents function, particularly regarding data access and processing. Confidential computing approaches are not a complete solution, and do not address these core concerns. In particular, these approaches still leave the power to determine the extent of privacy guarantees (if any) in the hands of these providers.

We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

In addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry.

Finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes. We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.

Signal Technology Foundation is the nonprofit home of the Signal app, which is trusted by millions around the world. We protect free expression and enable secure global communication through open source privacy technology. Signal Technology Foundation is a US 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization.

Don't have Signal? Give it a try!

items.title: Carnival Cruises emits ten times more sulphur oxide than all of Europe's cars (2019)
items.author: sammatilda
items.content:
In April, Ecohustler disrupted Carnival Cruise's AGM calling on the shareholders to reduce their company's pollution using straight forward and affordable methods - like burning cleaner fuel. Since then, a new report outlines the corporation's impact on the coastline of Europe. These vast floating cities are burning dirty bunker fuel and creating shocking levels of air pollution wherever they go. Shipping has been an unregulated industry for too long and action is urgently required.

Carnival Corporation, the world’s largest luxury cruise operator, emitted nearly 10 times more sulphur oxide (SOx) around European coasts than did all 260 million European cars in 2017, a new analysis by sustainable transport group Transport & Environment reveals.

Royal Caribbean Cruises, the world’s second largest, is second, yet four times worse than the European car fleet. SOx emissions form sulphate (SO4) aerosols that increase human health risks and contribute to acidification in terrestrial and aquatic environments.

SUPPORTED BY

JOIN US →

In absolute terms, Spain, Italy and Greece, closely followed by France and Norway, are the European countries most exposed to SOx air pollution from cruise vessels while Barcelona, Palma de Mallorca and Venice are the most impacted European port cities, followed by Civitavecchia (Rome) and Southampton.

All photos by Greg English ©

These countries are so exposed because they are major tourist destinations, but also because they have less stringent marine sulphur fuel standards which allows cruise ships to burn the dirtiest most sulphurous fuel all along their coastlines.

Faig Abbasov, shipping policy manager at T&E, said: “Luxury cruise ships are floating cities powered by some of the dirtiest fuel possible. Cities are rightly banning dirty diesel cars but they’re giving a free pass to cruise companies that spew out toxic fumes that do immeasurable harm both to those on board and on nearby shores. This is unacceptable.“

NOX emissions from cruise ships in Europe also heavily impact some cities, equivalent to about 15% of the nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted by Europe’s passenger car fleet in a year, the report finds. In Marseille, for example, 57 cruise ships emitted in 2017 almost as much NOx as one-quarter of the city’s 340,000 passenger cars. Along the coasts of countries such as Norway, Denmark, Greece, Croatia and Malta a handful of cruise ships are also responsible for more NOx than the majority of their domestic car fleet.

Europe should implement a zero-emission port standard as soon as possible, this could then be extended to other ship types. The report also recommends extending emission control areas (ECAs), currently in place only in the North and Baltic Seas and English Channel, to the rest of the European seas. Furthermore, the report recommends regulating NOx emissions from existing ships, which are currently exempt from NOx standards applying in emission control areas.

Faig Abbasov concluded “There are enough mature technologies to clean up cruise ships. Shore-side electricity can help cut in-port emissions, batteries are a solution for shorter distances and hydrogen technology can power even the biggest cruise ships. The cruise sector are apparently not willing to make the shift voluntarily, so we need governments to step in and mandate zero emission standards.”

items.title: Jujutsu Primer
items.author: renehsz
items.content:
provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover new powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.

If you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository, so you can try out on a repo on your own, without fully ejecting from .

Personally, I think considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.

Official installation instructions are here, but here are a few common methods:

In an existing repository, run:

From here on, and repo state will be synchronized automatically.

To set your user details globally, run commands like these:

You can edit ’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:

In addition to the scope, also has and scopes. View the merged config with:

A , also called a , is essentially the same thing as a commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.

When using a Git repo backend, the is the same as the commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of below, the hex hashes and on the right are commit IDs.


│  
│  Adjust config
~

The IDs on the left hand side ( and ) are , which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.

Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting , we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix .

We can inspect the commit with , using its short prefix .

Commit ID: 
Change ID: 
Bookmarks: 
Author   :  <> ()
Committer:  <> ()

    Adjust config

Let’s take another look at our commit graph:


│  
│  Adjust config
~

On commit , you’ll see the symbol on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our , or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways:

shows commit details and a diff, which is empty here. 

Commit ID: 
Change ID: 
Author   :  <> ()
Committer:  <> ()

shows repo state with diff stats. 

The working copy has no changes.
Working copy  (@) : 
Parent commit (@-): Adjust config

works much like . Its output is empty here, since there are no changes in the current working copy relative to the parent commit.

This output isn’t very interesting, since has no changes. Let’s make an example change to see what happens. If we edit and rerun , we see this:

Commit ID: 
Change ID: 
Author   :  <> ()
Committer:  <> ()



│  
│  Adjust config
~

You’ll notice several things have changed. The working copy has been automatically committed, and is no longer marked . The new commit ID for is , since we’ve added changes, but the change ID for is still . has no staging area like in , so we don’t have to manually add files. When we run a command to inspect or modify repo state after editing files, automatically snapshots the working copy as a new physical commit for the relevant logical change.

Let’s give this change a description (also called a commit message). We can either run , which opens an editor, or provide it directly with .

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      : Adjust config

Notice again that the commit ID has changed, since the hash covers the commit message, but the change ID has remained stable.

Now, let’s say we’re ready to use this new feature, and we want to organize that change in a separate commit. We can create a new commit with :

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      :  Implement the feature


│  
○  
│  Implement the feature

│  Adjust config
~

We’ve created an empty change on top of . reflects that we are editing this new revision which does not yet differ from its parent.

The working copy has no changes.
Working copy  (@) : 
Parent commit (@-):  Implement the feature

is a shorthand for this common and combo. Let’s make another change to use our new feature, and commit it.

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      :  Use the feature


│  
○  
│  Use the feature
○  
│  Implement the feature

│  Adjust config
~

To inspect the commit we just created (), we can no longer use the bare , which defaults to showing . We have to pass the revision we want to inspect:

Commit ID: 
Change ID: 
Author   :  <> ()
Committer:  <> ()

    Use the feature


 def my_new_feature():
   pass

We can describe empty commits to record intent before starting work. Let’s create a new commit on top of to remind ourselves that we need to document the feature.

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      :  Implement the feature
Added 0 files, modified 1 files, removed 0 files

A separate would also work just fine instead of the flag on . Here’s the current commit graph:


│  
│ ○  
├─┘  Use the feature
○  
│  Implement the feature

│  Adjust config
~

Note how we’ve created branching commits without creating a named branch. This highlights a major difference between ’s branchless model and ’s branch-centric model of organizing work streams. Instead of juggling your work-in-progress on branches, you work on a graph of commits. Once ready to share, you push branches to a Git forge from your commit graph (more on that later).

A revset, an idea borrowed from Mercurial, is an expression that selects a set of revisions from the commit graph. Most commands accept revsets in their arguments. When we ran , the argument was actually a trivial revset that resolved to the single change with ID . The command has an flag that we can use to preview a revset. Some demonstrative examples follow.

○  
│  Implement the feature
~


│  
~

│  Use the feature
~

Commits between and , inclusive:


│  
○  
│  Implement the feature

│  Adjust config
~

Commit and all descendants:


│  
│ ○  
├─┘  Use the feature
○  
│  Implement the feature
~

Commits authored by that also have ID or :


│  
○  
│  Implement the feature
~

I’ll defer to the official documentation for exhaustive detail. The Revsets language specification is easily my most referenced documentation page, so I would recommend skimming it to see what’s possible.

Let’s say in the course of documenting our feature in we realized we made a mistake in the implementation in parent change . We don’t need to manually commit or stash changes to switch tasks. We simply switch our working copy to with :

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      : Adjust config
Added 0 files, modified 0 files, removed 1 files

Our working copy once again shows the changes from .

Commit ID: 
Change ID: 
Author   :  <> ()
Committer:  <> ()

    Implement the feature

hasn’t lost track of the changes above our working copy, including our most recent edits to :

○  
│  Document the feature
│ ○  
├─┘  Use the feature

│  
│  Adjust config
~

Instead of switching commits with , we could have run . The revset is evaluated before switching the working copy, so this moves to the parent commit. The built-in commands and provide another way to move up and down a stack of commits.

If we edit files in the working copy, the descendant commits will be automatically rebased upon the next invocation. For example, if we edit ’s implementation in and then run , we’ll see that changes , , and all get new commit IDs. also tells us that it performed a rebase.

Rebased 2 descendant commits onto updated working copy.
○  
│  Document the feature
│ ○  
├─┘  Use the feature

│  
│  Adjust config
~

If the automatic rebase happened to cause merge conflicts, doesn’t require us to fix them immediately, like would. Instead, records that the commit is conflicted and lets you carry on with your current task. This is massively helpful to reduce mental context switching, as your stacked commits grow more complex.

Rebased 2 descendant commits onto updated working copy.
○  
│  Document the feature
│ 
├─┘  Use the feature

│  
│  Adjust config
~

To view the conflicts, we can edit the conflicted commit…

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      :  Implement the feature
Added 0 files, modified 1 files, removed 0 files

main.py

In a text editor, we can resolve these conflicts, and the next time we run any command, we’ll see that has marked the commit as unconflicted:

Working copy changes:

Working copy  (@) : 
Parent commit (@-):  Implement the feature

Let’s say we made a mistake in that conflict resolution, and we want to undo it. In , undoing an action, if it’s even possible, is often complicated. In , we can always run :

Undid operation:  () snapshot working copy
Restored to operation:  () edit commit e562bff4876f3ea76248c3f730e9e74d3e28e8a0
Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      :  Implement the feature
Added 0 files, modified 1 files, removed 0 files

main.py    
New conflicts appeared in 1 commits:
  To resolve the conflicts, start by creating a commit on top of
the conflicted commit:
  jj new 
Then use `jj resolve`, or edit the conflict markers in the file directly.
Once the conflicts are resolved, you can inspect the result with `jj diff`.
Then run `jj squash` to move the resolution into the conflicted commit.

More generally, maintains a history of all actions in . We can inspect this log and to a point in that history, or an individual operation. If the itself was a mistake, we can .

The in the output above is a bit of a spoiler for our next topic, the squash workflow.

Editing commits that have descendants can sometimes feel sketchy. If you’re iterating on a large diff that has left your working memory, it would be nice to separate your new changes from the existing diff. For example, we might like to inspect the diff that resolves a rebase conflict in isolation.

Let’s follow the instructions from the above output. We first create a new commit on top of the conflicted commit:

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      :  Use the feature

main.py    

│  
│  Use the feature
~

Now we can resolve the conflicts in in our editor, and rerun :


│  
│  Use the feature
~

We can inspect the diff in if we like, and when we’re happy with the conflict resolution, we can squash it into the parent commit:

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      :  Use the feature
Existing conflicts were resolved or abandoned from 1 commits.


│  
○  
│  Use the feature
~

The conflict is now resolved, and we can continue our work.

One of the powerful qualities of is that it makes diffs malleable like clay. With automatic rebase and the confidence inspired by , we can move, combine, drop, and split diffs with ease.

Let’s try a few operations on our current commit graph. Here’s the starting point.


│  
○  
│  Use the feature
│ ○  
├─┘  Document the feature
○  
│  Implement the feature

│  Adjust config
~

Let’s use to coerce our branching commit graph into a linear history. Let’s say the documentation commit () should go between the implementation () and the usage (). We could accomplish this by moving (and its empty descendant) on top of :

Rebased 2 commits to destination.
Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      :  Use the feature
Added 1 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files


│  
○  
│  Use the feature
○  
│  Document the feature
○  
│  Implement the feature

│  Adjust config
~

Another way to accomplish the same effect would be to use jj rebase -r q --before n. Many commands have multiple ways to specify revsets. documents these well.

Since arguments to flags are all revsets, we can write a revset that selects a sequence of commits or commit subgraph, and move it elsewhere in the graph.

If we wanted to insert a commit below , the most direct way is , but for demonstration purposes, we could alternatively create a new commit on top of and rebase on top:

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      : Adjust config
Added 0 files, modified 0 files, removed 2 files


│  
│ ○  
│ │  Use the feature
│ ○  
│ │  Document the feature
│ ○  
├─┘  Implement the feature

│  Adjust config
~

Rebased 3 commits to destination.

○  
│  Use the feature
○  
│  Document the feature
○  
│  Implement the feature

│  
│  Adjust config
~

If you enjoy using TUIs, provides a commit graph editor similar to for reordering commits.

If we decided documentation should be in the same commit as implementation, we can squash:

Rebased 1 descendant commits.

will open an editor and give us a chance to write a combined commit message.

○  
│  Use the feature
○  
│  Implement and document the feature

│  
│  Adjust config
~

To drop a commit from the graph, we can use . Let’s drop the preparation commit:

Abandoned 1 commits:
  
Rebased 2 descendant commits onto parents of abandoned commits.
Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      : Adjust config


│  
│ ○  
│ │  Use the feature
│ ○  
├─┘  Implement and document the feature

│  Adjust config
~

To abandon parts of a commit (hunks or changes to whole files), we can use the TUI (see docs).

The TUI allows us to take a commit and split it into two consecutive commits by selecting which files or hunks should go in the first. Let’s use it to split up implementation and documentation again with :

The jj-hunk project provides a means to automate commit splitting. If you are so inclined, agents are quite good at using this tool to split up commits into a sequence of smaller changes for easier review.

does not have a native concept of a branch, but it does have a primitive called bookmarks that map to Git branches. When we need to manipulate Git branches, we do it by way of bookmarks.

You can go pretty far using Git without realizing this, but a Git branch is just a pointer to a commit. explicitly models bookmarks this way. bookmarks are essentially a named label attached to a commit that we can move around as we modify our commit graph, and push to/pull from a remote.

We’ll discuss a few basic workflows around Git branches below, but you can find a more complete guide in the docs on Working with GitHub.

Assuming we initialized in a git repository that has remotes, we should have some output for .

Since is branchless, the commits we’ve created locally don’t have a branch name. Luckily, doesn’t require us to pick one, and generates one for us. Generated branch names free you from thinking of a unique branch name so you can instead focus on writing a good commit message (usually the more durable descriptor of a change).

To create a generated bookmark for change ID and push up a corresponding Git branch, we can run a command like the following:

Now shows our change with a correspondingly named bookmark associated:

○  
│  Use the feature
~

We’re free to create a PR from this branch on GitHub now. You can customize the bookmark naming scheme with the template config documented here. It’s a common pattern to format branch names like <author name>/<change ID>.

Since creates a branch name that corresponds to a change ID, it seems to encourage one evolving change per PR. I think it’s usually best to lean into these ergonomics, and have one change per PR.

To update a branch, the general process is to either squash commits into a change that is already bookmarked, or create new commits and move the bookmark forward.

If you choose to squash commits into an existing bookmark (recommended to keep one change per PR), the flow is as follows.

First, create a new commit on top of our branch. 

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      : Use the feature
Added 2 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files

Working copy changes:

Working copy  (@) : 
Parent commit (@-): Use the feature

Squash them into the bookmark branch. 

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      : Use the feature

We now see has an asterisk next to it, indicating it has changes that haven’t been pushed to the remote. So let’s push them. 

Changes to push to origin:
  bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move sideways from b1284f61c417 to aeb869aef99b]

The remote branch now reflects the new changes. The above output says that we moved the branch sideways from one commit to another commit, which reflects that we did a force-push. runs the equivalent of a git push --force-with-lease, so if you’re ever unclear about what a push operation would do, you can use the flag. protects you against most dangerous force pushes refusing to rewrite a configurable revset of immutable commits. The default immutable revset is sensible, but you can make it more or less conservative by configuring your own immutable heads.

In this flow, we add new commits on top of our bookmark and then move the bookmark to point to our new commit.

Let’s first prepare the new commit. 

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      : Use the feature

Working copy changes:

Working copy  (@) : 
Parent commit (@-): Use the feature

Working copy  (@) now at: 
Parent commit (@-)      :  Add a usage example

The bookmark does not automatically move to our new commit. This is the biggest difference between bookmarks and Git branches. For now still points at the commit below:


│  
○  
│  Add a usage example
○  
│  Use the feature
~

There are several ways to move the bookmark to the new commit. The easiest is probably , which moves the closest bookmark to the given commit:

Advanced 1 bookmarks to Add a usage example

Now we’re ready to push the moved bookmark.

Changes to push to origin:
  bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move forward from aeb869aef99b to 2341ee4aa554]

Since is branchless, strictly speaking, we don’t “check out” a branch, but we can create a commit on top of a remote branch. First do the equivalent of a , importing remote bookmarks:

And create a new empty commit on top of the remote branch:

Our working copy now contains all the commits on the remote branch. However, if we were to drop back to , we see that from ’s perspective, we’re in a detached head state, not on any branch.

Not currently on any branch.
nothing to commit, working tree clean

This is because is editing a commit above a bookmark, and does not have an equivalent to ’s “current branch” state.

Syncing with the trunk (e.g. ) is just a specific example of this flow. We would to update our to the upstream , and then rebase our commits on top. For example, the following would rebase on top of a new :

commit graph manipulation is easiest when you have a live commit graph on screen. There are different ways you can accomplish this.

jjui is a TUI for that allows you to edit the visual graph directly. I have not personally used this, but I know people who like it.

I prefer to have an always-live in the corner of my screen by way of viddy (a nicer version of that supports color):

I recommend filtering down this log to a revset that represents your current work. Here’s a starting point:

You might also consider trying my experimental project jj-stamp, which is a local code review GUI for the squash workflow. Even if you don’t use the squash review workflow, it makes a pretty good diff viewer with a live on the side and a terminal for running operations.

One of the biggest productivity gains from comes in its ability to support stacked PR workflows. This merits its own post, so I’ll keep it short.

Large changes are easier to understand when they’re broken up into a series of logical steps. Breaking up a large change into smaller sequential atoms of review makes the whole change easier to understand. Stacked PRs attempt to leverage this fact to optimize merge throughput, while simultaneously removing pipeline stalls in the review process.

Let’s say we’re building a new feature. We can decide we want to split up implementation into three stages:

  1. Refactor to make the feature easier to implement
  2. Use the feature in another system

’s ability to work on stacked changes with automatic rebase is a natural fit for implementing these three stages. Each of the three stages maps to a single commit, each with an associated bookmark/branch/PR:

○  
│  Use the feature
○  
│  Implement the feature
○  
│  Refactor for the feature
~

After you implement the first change, you can put up a PR for review and immediately start working on the next change. Your work stream becomes a long queue where you pop off the bottom as PRs are ready to merge and push to the top, with no pipeline stalls.

It’s pretty easy to manually set up small PR stacks with and GitHub, but once you get hooked on the technique (making stacks 5–10 PRs deep), you’ll want a tool. is my entry into the ring of stacked PR tools. More on that soon.

  • Steve Klabnik’s tutorial was my first introduction to . I don’t think it’s maintained as a durable resource (and I don’t promise mine will be!), but it’s still a good read.
  • I follow the releases RSS feed. Lately the releases have been packed with new features. Overall is quite stable, but the occasional bug is fixed promptly.
  • The blog of East River Source Control, a company that is building a new forge and code review platform intended to support Jujutsu well. The creator of Jujutsu, Martin von Zweigbergk, has joined as the CTO, and they have lots of other smart people as well. Perhaps a successor to GitHub one day? I’m rooting for them.
  • My personal config. You might find some useful aliases or tricks here, but I haven’t attempted to make it readable.

If you find FFmpeg useful, you are welcome to contribute by donating. More downloading options

Since FFmpeg is developed with Git, multiple repositories from developers and groups of developers are available.

All FFmpeg releases are cryptographically signed with our public PGP key and should be verified for authenticity. 

pub   rsa2048 2011-04-26 [SC]
    FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8
uid           [  full  ] FFmpeg release signing key <ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org>
sub   rsa2048 2011-04-26 [E]
  1. Import our public key into your local keyring: 
    $ curl https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-devel.asc | gpg --import
  2. Download a release tarball and its corresponding signature.
  3. Verify the signature: 
    $ gpg --verify ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz.asc ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz
gpg: Signature made Sun 21 Feb 2021 06:35:15 AEST
gpg:                using RSA key FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8
gpg:                issuer "ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org"
gpg: Good signature from "FFmpeg release signing key <ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org>" [full]
Optionally, you can verify that git and tarball match, the only differences should be the absence of .git* files in the tarball and a VERSION file in the tarball containing the version. The git tags should be signed with EDDSA key DD1EC9E8DE085C629B3E1846B18E8928B3948D64

A release that also has a file carries post-quantum signatures (RFC 9980) made with both of these keys:

GnuPG cannot verify these yet; use sq 1.4 or later built with a cryptographic backend that supports these algorithms (OpenSSL 3.5 or RustCrypto), both of these must succeed: 

$ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-mldsa87-ed448.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz
$ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-slhdsa256s.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz

items.title: PostgreSQL 19
items.author: linzhangrun
items.content:
• Issue a warning after successful MD5 password authentication (Nathan Bossart) §

    The warning can be disabled via server variable . MD5 passwords were marked as deprecated in 18.

  • Remove support (Thomas Munro) §

    only supported over , which is unfixably insecure.

  • Dumps created using pre- 19 versions of or , and using standard_conforming_strings = off, will not properly load into 19 and later servers. Users should create dumps using 19 or later versions of these applications, or use standard_conforming_strings = on.

    Client applications still support operations with servers having standard_conforming_strings = off, for compatibility with old servers. The server variable has been removed as unnecessary.

  • Disallow carriage returns and line feeds in database, role, and tablespace names (Mahendra Singh Thalor) §

    will also disallow upgrading of clusters that use such names. This was changed to avoid security problems.

  • The values of such columns were not well-defined.

  • Change a call which returns no rows to return an empty array (Richard Guo) §

    This previously returned .

  • Cause transactions to pass their and status to postgres_fdw sessions (Etsuro Fujita) §

    This means transactions can no longer modify rows processed by postgres_fdw sessions.

  • Lock size allocation has changed, so effectively settings must now be doubled to match their capacity in previous releases.

  • Remove server variable (Thomas Munro) §

  • Change to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) §

    Previously was enabled by default, and activated based on optimizer costs, but this costing has been determined to be unreliable. This change requires sites that are doing many large analytical queries to manually enable .

  • Change parallel vacuum leaders and workers to share the cost-based vacuum delay limit (Bharath Rupireddy) §

    Previously each worker process slept based only on the cost it incurred itself, so a parallel vacuum could consume several times the budget set by . With this change, with parallel workers and cost-based delay enabled might run slower than in previous releases.

  • This is necessary since sequence errors are now tracked separately.

  • Rename wait event to and rename wait event to (Andres Freund) §

  • Remove wait event and add more precise wait events , , and (Andres Freund) §

  • Change index access method handlers to use a static structure, rather than dynamically allocated ones (Matthias van de Meent) §

  • Remove optimizer hook get_relation_info_hook and add better-placed hook build_simple_rel_hook (Robert Haas) §

  • Change 's command to honor the setting (Chao Li) §

  • Change full text search and to use the database's locale provider for character classification when parsing text (Jeff Davis) §

    Previously, characters were classified using libc, regardless of the locale provider. In databases with a locale provider other than libc (e.g., , ) and where the locale configured through that locale provider behaves differently from the setting configured for the database, particularly a LC_CTYPE of , the output of some full text search and functions could change. When upgrading such databases using , it is recommended to reindex all indexes which use full text search and after the upgrade, and to recompute any stored values.

  • Change how fuzzystrmatch functions handle non- characters (Peter Eisentraut, Jeff Davis) §§

    and now upper-case their input using the database's default collation rather than always using libc, and , , and now treat only letters as letters. When upgrading with , it is recommended to reindex any indexes that use these functions after the upgrade.

  • Remove encoding (Thomas Munro) §

    This encoding was complex and rarely used. Databases using it will need to be dumped and restored with a different encoding.

items.content:
EXTRA, extra! Today I’m launching Future Stories, my own podcast about technology, science and the way we live.

TCP/IP

left Google this yearHis words: “the speed of light is too slow.”

bug related one (ring a bell? those never stopped over the years…)

“what if they screw it up?”

The thread is public

We didn’t go very deep into AI. Time was short, and it’s not his main field these days. But even there, he has a clear way of thinking about it. And near the end he shows a piece of the original ARPANET on camera, and talks about his worry that the next century won’t be able to read what we leave behind.

“I’m worried that the 22nd century won’t know what happened in the 21st because all of our records will have evaporated or will be uninterpretable.”

The full conversation is 56 minutes, with chapters:

ourfuturestories.eu/#contact

50 years of the TCP paperYou can listen here

The paper is “A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication”, by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, published in May 1974 in IEEE Transactions on Communications. It described TCP, a way to join many packet networks into a network of networks. TCP was later split into TCP and IP, and in 1983 they became the core of the Internet that DARPA launched.

items.title: ChatGPT for SNES
items.author: evan_
items.content:
Download the v0.7 ROM (1.5 MB zip: one .sfc file). Requires a flash cart with Super FX support, such as an FXPak Pro or an sd2snes with current firmware. Leave Chip Options › SuperFX speed at Normal. The build with the fact book (17 MB zip: the .sfc and its .msu file) also needs MSU-1 support: put both files in the same folder with their names unchanged.

  • ChatGPT for SNES is an unofficial experiment designed by Benj Edwards and coded by AI agents: a ChatGPT-style chat program for the Super Nintendo. Its training conversations were written by gpt-oss-120b, OpenAI's open-weight model. Not made or endorsed by OpenAI.
  • This is version 0.7 (2 November 2026).
  • A small language model with about 2.2 million parameters runs on the cartridge's Super FX 2 chip and writes its answers one word at a time.
  • In the main build every word it writes comes from the language model. A second build adds a fact book (the opening sentences of 150,000 Simple English Wikipedia articles, stored in the cartridge's MSU-1 data file): like ChatGPT searching the web, its model can decide to look something up and print what the book says.
  • Here it runs in the Snes9x emulator in your browser; the first visit loads about 4 MB (19 MB with the fact book).
  • Press Start (Enter) on the title screen, then type on your keyboard and press Enter to send. Each letter takes a moment to appear, because the page moves the cursor on the game's own on-screen keyboard.
  • It is not a useful assistant: the model is millions of times smaller than the models behind ChatGPT, knows about 8,000 words, and often gets things wrong, sometimes confidently. The fact book can carry mistakes too.

If you liked this, you might enjoy Séance, which runs a tiny AI language model on a real NES.
