items.title: Cooling buildings is overtaking heating them as an energy need, IEA says
items.author: robtherobber
items.content:
The energy needed to cool the world’s buildings is overtaking the energy needed to heat them for the first time in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on November 19, 2026. The IEA, an intergovernmental agency that advises governments on energy, made the finding in the World Energy Outlook 2026, its main annual report. “Already today, for the first time in energy history, demand for cooling in buildings is overtaking that for heating,” the report’s executive summary says.

Two forces drive the change: rising incomes and rising temperatures. In emerging and developing economies outside China, 85% of households are exposed to high temperatures for at least part of the year. Fewer than one in five households there own an air conditioner.

In the IEA’s main scenario, a projection built on the policies governments have announced, the electricity used for cooling worldwide grows by 1,700 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2035. A terawatt-hour is a billion kilowatt-hours; the kilowatt-hour is the unit on a household power bill. That increase is roughly India’s total electricity demand today.

A first in energy history

The IEA’s press release calls the shift “a striking milestone”: “energy needs to keep buildings cool are now overtaking energy needs for heating them for the first time in history.”

Most of this year’s report deals with the oil and gas shock caused by disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The cooling finding comes from another part of the report, on what people use energy for: getting around, heating, cooling and computing. The IEA calls these uses energy services.

Of these services, cooling adds the most new demand. Cooling demand in buildings has risen 55% since 2015, the IEA says in its full report. In every scenario the agency models, cooling accounts for more than 40% of the growth in energy services worldwide through 2035.

That growth comes mostly from hot countries that are getting richer. It also comes from places where cooling used to be a minor need. The report names Europe, where heat waves and warmer summers are turning cooling into a new source of demand. It cites record heat waves there and strong air conditioner sales in European countries that historically needed little cooling.

Who has air conditioning, and who doesn’t

Air conditioner ownership varies widely. In Australia, Japan and the United States, around 90% of households own at least one unit, according to the report. In India and Indonesia, fewer than one in five do, despite high cooling needs. Worldwide, around 80% of the population lives in places that need cooling for at least part of the year, and around 40% of households own an air conditioner.

In emerging and developing economies outside China, the IEA projects that ownership will rise from under 20% of households today to 32% by 2035 and 45% by 2050. The projection is the same in all its scenarios. The IEA also models a current policies scenario, which counts only the policies already in place. In that scenario, more than 85% of the growth in the world’s stock of home air conditioners over the next decade happens in emerging and developing economies, China included.

By the middle of the century, the IEA projects, the world’s buildings will have more cooled floor space than heated floor space.

More electricity for cooling, and a heat-wave what-if

In the main scenario, which the IEA calls the Stated Policies Scenario, the electricity used to cool buildings rises by 1,700 TWh by 2035. It goes from about 3,000 TWh a year today to 4,700 TWh a year.

The report also models a “heatwave case,” a what-if kept apart from the main scenario. In it, heat waves become stronger, more frequent and longer, so more households buy air conditioners and use them more. In that case, cooling demand grows by 700 TWh more than in the main scenario by 2035. That is 40% more growth.

Cooling also weighs more on power grids than its share of total use suggests. Air conditioners run hardest at the same time, on the hottest days. That drives up peak demand, the highest demand a grid must meet during the year. In the main scenario, cooling makes up only 12% of the world’s electricity demand in 2035, but 30% of peak demand.

Peak demand is measured in gigawatts (GW), which count power at a single moment, while terawatt-hours count energy used over a period. Added up across the world’s power systems, it is 4,700 GW today. It grows by about 40% by 2035, in both the main scenario and the current policies scenario. Under current policies, the cooling part of the peak alone grows by 720 GW, more than India’s entire power generating capacity today.

In the main scenario, cooling and appliances together add 2,900 TWh of electricity demand by 2035. That is more electricity than the whole European Union uses today. Almost 90% of that growth happens in emerging and developing economies.

Heating still consumes more energy

Measured by the fuel and electricity consumed, heating is still well ahead. “Globally, there is less cooling than heating demand, but more electric cooling than electric heating demand,” the report says in its section on buildings. Space heating, which keeps rooms warm, uses about a third of all the energy consumed in buildings, more than any other use.

The milestone uses a different yardstick. In the report’s framing, the comparison is about energy services, meaning the comfort delivered. The sentence about cooling overtaking heating sits in the report’s section on demand for energy services. The IEA measures those services as “useful energy”: the energy that does the job people want, such as “the heat produced by a heater.”

By our reading, the two findings fit together because of how the equipment works. A boiler burns fuel and loses part of its energy in the process. An air conditioner, like a heat pump, moves heat from one place to another, so it delivers more cooling than the electricity it consumes.

The report counts air conditioners and heat pumps as devices whose output exceeds the energy they take in. That, by our reading, is why cooling can overtake heating in the service delivered while heating still consumes more energy.

The executive summary puts no number on the crossing itself. It is a result of the IEA’s modeling, and the agency describes the crossing as under way (“is overtaking”). None of the report’s scenarios is a forecast, as the IEA’s executive director, Fatih Birol, said in the press release.

In advanced economies, heating remains the largest energy service. It declines only slowly, as better insulation and warmer average temperatures offset the effect of rising incomes.

Air conditioners are spreading in the countries where most of the world’s people live. In the IEA’s projections, the share of households that own one in emerging and developing economies outside China more than doubles by 2050. Those households gain comfort, and power grids must carry a bigger load in the hottest hours of the year. Electric trucks, cars and heat pumps add to the load on those grids as well.

Electricity already supplied 23% of the energy consumed worldwide in 2025, and the IEA sees that share closing in on 30% by 2035. The agency says at least 25 million kilometers of new power lines are needed over the next ten years. On the supply side, solar covered more of the growth in world energy demand in 2025 than any other source, a first for a renewable source, according to the IEA. In the European Union, solar became the biggest source of electricity over the summer.

Efficiency rules also shape demand. Minimum efficiency standards are the legal floor on how efficient an appliance must be to go on sale. For household appliances such as refrigerators, washing machines, lighting and televisions, the IEA calculates that bringing every country up to the strictest standards in force today would save 800 TWh of electricity by 2035, almost half of it from refrigerators alone. For cooling, the current policies scenario keeps those standards at today’s levels, and cooling demand reaches 4,900 TWh by 2035, compared with 4,700 TWh in the main scenario.

items.title: How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40k staff
items.author: liotier
items.content:
The European Commission went from a Matrix proof of concept in December 2025 to a sovereign communication tool rolled out to every Commission laptop by September 2026. That tool, built on Matrix by Element, and run by the Commission itself, now serves more than 40,000 users.

At The Matrix Conference 2026, Diana Gheorghe, Head of Sector for Digital Workplace Communication and Collaboration Services, and Alexandru Vignide, Service Delivery Manager for the Commission's sovereign communication tool, told the story of how they got there. The pair were transparent about what got harder at scale, and how they dealt with it.

Sovereignty means more than where the servers sit

“Sovereignty” can have a different meaning for different people and organisations, so the Commission started by pinning down what it means for them. Their answer spans five dimensions: resilience and business continuity, vendor diversity, control over their data, ownership of the platform, and leverage in procurement - the ability to negotiate with, or walk away from, a supplier. That last one is easy to forget, and arguably the one that bites hardest when it's missing.

For internal communications specifically, the priorities were resilience, data ownership and, crucially, interoperability. That's what led them to Matrix: an open protocol whose value lies in letting separate systems talk to each other. They chose Element Server Suite Pro (ESS Pro), Element's enterprise distribution of Matrix, as a mature implementation, and decided to host, operate and architect the service under their own control.

Sovereign cloud hosting, familiar login, without federation (yet)

With the building blocks chosen, Alexandru walked through three architecture decisions.

The service doesn't run in a Commission-owned data centre. Instead it runs with sovereign cloud providers selected through the sovereign hosting tender awarded earlier this year, in order to meet its sovereignty and hosting requirements. Sovereign doesn't have to mean building everything in-house; it means choosing who you depend on, and on what terms.

The deployment is integrated with EU Login, the sign-in staff already use every day. A new tool is easier to adopt when logging in feels familiar.

Connecting to Matrix servers outside the Commission is still under assessment. The technical side is being explored - there was a separate hands-on demo using non-production environments at the conference - but federation also needs governance, participation and structure, which takes longer to agree than a config change.

The Commission started working with Matrix in summer 2025, or, as Alexandru put it, at last year's Matrix Conference. From there, things moved quickly:

  1. the architecture and engineering team delivered a proof of concept showing Matrix and Element were viable for the Commission. It earned a green light for a Commission-wide service, which Alexandru described as a nice Christmas present.
  2. the team built the production infrastructure, along with the hosting and operations needed to run it, and was ready by June.
  3. a laptop pilot covering both the desktop and web clients, followed by a mobile pilot through the Commission's mobile device management (MDM) platform.
  4. the laptop rollout to all Commission users, delivered in waves, was and completed in September.

The Commission is now exploring a mobile rollout, and what federation could look like.

Scaling to 40,000 users brought challenges

Rolling out to 40,000 people surfaces problems no pilot will. Alexandru described the four main ones his team ran into, and how they tackled each.

Finding colleagues across servers. The Commission runs several Synapse homeservers, and early on, people on different servers couldn't always find each other. The Commission's teams worked with Element to fix this, and now a plain user search finds anyone in the Commission, whichever server they're on.

Accounts that only appear after sign-up. The Commission chose user-led account creation rather than pre-provisioning every account. The catch is that you can't find a colleague who hasn't registered yet, which made the discovery problem above feel worse while adoption was still ramping up.

Live presence was switched off. As more users came on board, the load from live presence (the real-time “online/away” indicator) started to affect performance, so the team disabled it. They're now looking at a user status feature being developed with Element as the replacement.

Infrastructure had to learn to scale itself. Rolling out in waves over three months meant uneven, shifting demand, so the team tuned the infrastructure to adjust automatically.

Running through all of this was the balance between security and usability. Most of the hardening work was done with the Commission's security teams before the rollout, and continues through regular security reviews and continuous improvements. The team made sure that hardening didn't get in the way of everyday tasks like creating an account, recovering it or verifying a new device, and documented those steps clearly for staff. Feedback from tickets, internal forums and public channels is consolidated into prioritised goals for the Commission's own roadmap.

The most common question, Diana said, is whether Element is meant to replace Microsoft Teams, or consumer apps like Signal and WhatsApp. The short answer: neither, directly. Element is positioned as an internal communication tool for specific use cases - secure communication among them - where the Commission's existing stack doesn't fully meet its needs. Teams bundles communication, collaboration and a whole platform behind it, so there's no one-to-one swap to be had.

That makes expectation-setting part of the job. People naturally compare workplace tools with the apps they use at home and go looking for feature-for-feature matches. Diana's view is that this mindset is something to address head-on in any organisational change: Element is a tool in its own right, with its own feature set, that the Commission and Element can evolve together.

Part of the goal is to bring work conversations onto a tool the Commission controls. 

Federation goes beyond tech

The Commission has been interested in federation for a long time. The obvious starting point is other EU institutions, but it wouldn't stop there: the Commission also works closely with member states, governments and non-governmental organisations.

No decision has been made yet, and the Commission is taking it one step at a time. First comes the technical question of what the technology can actually do, because, as Diana put it, there's no point writing policies technology can't deliver. Then comes governance: who the partners would be, on what terms, with what scope, and how security and privacy are handled.

Alexandru ended the talk by sharing what the deployment had taught the Commission.

Sovereignty is operational. It depends on operational control and the trustworthiness of the whole chain of partners, not just on where the service is hosted.

Adoption depends on everyday usability. Discoverability, onboarding support and everything around the product shape whether people use it.

Interoperability needs more than technology. It also needs clear structure, participation and governance.

He also noted that introducing a new communication tool has been a journey, and still is. Along the way, the Commission has relied on trustworthy service providers, and he described the collaboration with Element as a success.

items.title: SSD prices may begin to decline in the latter half of 2027
items.author: illidan1000
items.content:
It is the question we get asked more than any other right now, and it is the most searched phrase that brings people to this blog. So here is the straight answer: SSD prices should start to ease in the second half of 2027. Hard drives will take longer, probably into 2028, because the factories that make them have already sold that output.

That is not a guess. It comes from the analysts who track memory contract prices every quarter, and from what Seagate and Western Digital told their own investors this summer. Below we lay out the evidence, explain why spinning drives and SSDs are running on different clocks, and give you a realistic timeline with the signals to watch.

While you wait, the cheapest terabyte is the one you already own. DriveVault scans each of your external drives once and keeps a searchable catalogue of everything on them, so you can see free space, spot duplicate project folders and find old files without plugging anything in. For a lot of people that audit pushes the next drive purchase back by months, which is exactly what you want when prices are at a record.

Waiting for prices to fall? Use what you have first. DriveVault catalogues every drive you own so you can search them offline, find free space and spot duplicates before you buy.
Download Free

NAND supply is forecast to catch up with demand from mid-2027. Expect a gradual slide, not a crash.

Capacity is contracted into 2028 and no new factories are planned. Relief comes via bigger drives, slowly.

  • Prices are still rising, just more slowly. A year into the crisis, hard drives cost 134% more than in September 2025 and SSDs 129% more, in ComputerBase's tracking.
  • TrendForce expects the NAND shortage to end in the second half of 2027.
  • Hard drives are booked up. Seagate has most of its data centre capacity allocated into 2028, and neither it nor Western Digital is building new factories.
  • 2024 prices are not coming back soon. Contracts now include pricing, and AI demand is still growing.
  • Need storage for work? Buy it. Buying speculatively? Wait, and favour SSDs, which should get cheaper first.

Where Prices Stand in September 2026

Before looking forward, it helps to be honest about where we are. The German tech site ComputerBase has priced the same dozen popular drives every month since mid-September 2025, which makes its tracker one of the cleanest before-and-after records of this crisis. Its one-year check, published today, shows hard drives averaging 134% above their pre-crisis prices, up from 129% a month earlier. SSDs are 129% higher, up from 126%. Both are new records.

(HDD)
(HDD)

Source: ComputerBase price check, 16 September 2026. German retail prices, excluding eBay and Amazon Marketplace sellers.

The pattern in that table matters. The biggest hard drives, the 18TB to 24TB models that data centres also buy, have risen fastest. The smaller desktop drives most creatives actually use have "only" doubled. If you are shopping for a budget external drive, you are feeling the mild end of this.

The one encouraging detail: the monthly increases have shrunk to a few percentage points. Prices are still climbing, but the curve is flattening. That is usually the first stage before a market turns.

Why Hard Drives and SSDs Will Recover at Different Times

Most coverage lumps "storage prices" together. That hides the most useful part of the answer, because hard drives and SSDs are made by different companies, in different factories, and sold in different ways.

SSDs follow the chip market

SSDs are built from NAND flash chips made by Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Those chips are priced quarter by quarter in contract negotiations, and some trade on a spot market that moves weekly. When supply catches up, SSD prices can respond within a couple of quarters. They went up fast. They can come down reasonably fast too.

Hard drives follow multi-year contracts

Hard drives come from essentially two companies, Seagate and Western Digital, with Toshiba a distant third. Almost all of their output now goes to cloud providers on long-term agreements. Those agreements lock in volume and, crucially, price for years at a time. That is why hard drive prices rose later and more steadily than SSDs, and it is why they will be slower to fall.

The SSD Timeline: What the Analysts Say

TrendForce is the most widely cited memory pricing firm, and its forecasts have been the best guide through this cycle. Here is how its view has shifted during 2026.

Then came the forecast that actually answers the question. In its July NAND update, TrendForce said the market would run a 4 to 5% supply deficit through 2026, then move back into balance in the second half of 2027. The reasons it gives are ordinary ones: manufacturers squeezing more bits out of existing fabs, steady output growth, and consumer demand staying weak because everything costs so much. It expects notebook shipments to fall around 10% this year and shrink again in 2027.

New supply is also arriving from China. YMTC reached around 14% of global NAND shipments in the second quarter and has told investors it wants to be the world's largest NAND maker by the end of 2027, backed by a planned $4.9 billion share listing. Even if it falls short of that target, that much extra flash entering the market is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes SSD prices down.

Balance is not the same as cheap. TrendForce also warns that memory contract prices will remain broadly elevated in 2027, with cloud providers' spending projected to rise another 50% next year. And it flags that a breakthrough in agentic AI could soak up the extra supply. A market in balance means prices stop rising and start drifting down. It does not mean a return to 2024.

The Hard Drive Timeline: Booked Into 2028

For spinning drives, the most reliable evidence is what the two big manufacturers said on their earnings calls this summer. It is not encouraging for anyone hoping for a quick drop.

Seagate reported its fiscal year results on 28 July, with a record 52.7% gross margin. On the call, management said data centres now take around 90% of the capacity it ships, and that the vast majority of its high-capacity drive output is now allocated into calendar 2028. Seagate also told investors it has contracts setting both product configuration and pricing for the whole of 2027, and that it is not adding drive manufacturing capacity. Its plan is to cram more data onto each disk instead.

Western Digital tells the same story. Its fourth-quarter revenue rose 44% year on year, while the amount of storage it shipped rose only 22%. The gap is price. According to analysis of the earnings call, the company's average price per terabyte rose by a high-teens percentage, and its long-term agreements run through 2027 with two major customers and through 2028 with one, with price terms attached.

Put simply: the companies are sold out, they are making record margins, their contracts fix prices into 2028, and they have chosen not to build more factories. None of those conditions produce falling retail prices.

So where does hard drive relief come from?

Density. Seagate's HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) drives already make up around 40% of its data centre capacity shipments, and Western Digital plans full-scale HAMR production in 2027. As the cloud giants move to 36TB, 40TB and larger drives, the cost per terabyte falls for everyone, and older production lines can eventually be freed up for the consumer and mid-capacity drives you and I buy. That is a slow, grinding process. It points to prices levelling off through 2027 and easing from 2028, rather than a sudden correction.

Pulling all of that together, here is our best reading of how the next two years should play out. Treat it as a forecast, not a promise. Every forecast in this cycle so far has been revised at least once.

    What Could Change the Timeline

    AI infrastructure spending cools, Chinese NAND output ramps faster than expected, or consumer demand stays so weak that manufacturers start discounting to move stock. Module makers are already sitting on higher inventories because shoppers have stopped buying, which is the kind of pressure that eventually breaks prices.

    agentic AI takes off and data centres start storing far more data per user, if more manufacturers follow Micron's Crucial brand out of the consumer market, or if trade restrictions tighten on Chinese memory makers.

    • A flat or falling quarter in TrendForce's NAND contract survey. That would be the first since the crisis began, and the clearest sign SSD relief is on its way.
    • ComputerBase's monthly price check going negative for SSDs or hard drives. It publishes mid-month and is a good public scoreboard.
    • New SSD launches at the same or lower prices than the models they replace. The recent Samsung P9 and P7 did the opposite.
    • Seagate or Western Digital mentioning pricing pressure or customers delaying orders. So far, both say demand visibility is improving.

    Should You Buy Now or Wait?

    That depends entirely on why you need the storage. Here is how we would think about it.

    You need storage for paid work this year

    Waiting has no clear end date, and a lost booking costs more than the price premium. Buy what the job needs, not more. Our 4TB drive roundup and rugged 4TB SSD guide focus on value at today's prices.

    Your backups are incomplete

    A failed drive with no second copy is far more expensive than any price spike, especially when a replacement costs double. A basic spinning drive is still the cheapest way to hold a second copy. Just make sure the backup is actually complete. Our guide to verifying a backup drive shows how.

    You want a fast SSD upgrade that can wait

    SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first. If your current setup works, holding off until the second half of 2027 is a reasonable bet. You are accepting the risk that prices plateau rather than fall.

    You are stockpiling "just in case"

    Buying spare capacity at record prices, to sit empty on a shelf, is the worst trade in this market. You would be paying the peak for storage you might not need until prices have eased.

    Before You Buy Anything, Audit What You Have

    The most useful thing you can do while prices are this high is find out exactly what is on the drives you already own. Most creatives with a few years of work behind them have a drawer of drives, a few with duplicate project folders, and at least one nobody is quite sure about. DriveVault turns that pile into a catalogue you can search in seconds, even when the drives are unplugged.

    • See real free space across every drive before assuming you need a new one.
    • Find duplicate folders across drives with drive comparison, and reclaim the space safely.
    • Confirm a backup is complete before you wipe and reuse the original drive.
    • Share the catalogue with your team so nobody buys a drive to hold footage that already exists. See sharing drive catalogues.

    If you want a system for keeping it that way, our guide to organising multiple external drives covers naming, folder templates and archiving. Every terabyte you recover now is one you do not have to buy at 2026 prices.

    Frequently Asked Questions

    When will hard drive prices come down?

    Probably not before 2028 in any meaningful way. Seagate says the vast majority of its data centre hard drive capacity is already allocated into calendar 2028, and Western Digital has long-term agreements with price terms running through 2027 and 2028. Neither company is adding factory capacity. Relief is more likely to come from higher-capacity HAMR drives lowering the cost per terabyte than from a sudden price cut.

    When will SSD prices come down?

    TrendForce expects the NAND flash market to stay in a 4 to 5 percent supply deficit through 2026 and to move back into balance in the second half of 2027. That makes late 2027 the earliest realistic window for SSD prices to start falling, with gradual easing rather than a sharp drop.

    Will hard drive and SSD prices go back to 2024 levels?

    Not within the next two years on current evidence. Manufacturers have signed multi-year contracts that include pricing, and AI data centres now account for most of their output. Prices should ease from their peak, but planning around a return to 2024 prices is not supported by any current forecast.

    Should I buy a hard drive now or wait?

    If you need the storage for paid work or your backups are incomplete, buy now, because waiting for hard drive prices has no clear end date. If you are buying extra capacity speculatively, SSDs are the category most likely to get cheaper first, from the second half of 2027. Either way, audit the drives you already own first, since duplicated files often free up more space than people expect.

    Why are hard drives so expensive in 2026?

    AI data centres are buying almost all of the high-capacity drives Seagate and Western Digital can build, under long-term contracts. Data centres now take around 90 percent of Seagate's shipped capacity. With consumer products a small slice of their business and no new factories planned, retail prices have more than doubled since September 2025 in ComputerBase's tracking.

    Storage prices will come down. Just not yet, and not evenly. SSDs are on track to turn first, from the second half of 2027, as new flash supply catches up and consumer demand stays weak. Hard drives are locked into contracts that run into 2028, and their recovery will be slower and quieter, carried by bigger drives rather than price cuts.

    The practical move for the next year is simple. Buy what you genuinely need, skip the stockpile, and get every usable terabyte out of the drives already on your desk. We will update this article as the forecasts change.

    DriveVault catalogues your entire drive library so you can search, compare and find free space on any drive, even when it is not plugged in. Free to download on macOS.

items.title: Do not buy RAM, compress
items.author: Ecno92
items.content:
AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations. Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option. Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in , a solution to compress memory.

Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it. Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM. Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default. Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines. Most other distributions do not have it enabled.

Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes. What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4.

I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app. Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression. This could have cut our Cloud spend in half!

I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. (I have 32GB with some reserved for the graphics)

Nice to see the conversation and I hope that some of you started experimenting with compressing memory. Making more efficient use of the available resources is something important to understand as a community.

Two articles were mentioned that I think are a very important addition. While zram works fine for my situation, they advocate that is the better option for most situations. After reading both articles I agree with this conclusion.

items.title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite
items.author: ghostfoxgod
items.content:
We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.

On Kite, our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes.

Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB (ssdb), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years.

Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement:

  1. SSDB became unmaintained, which was an obvious operational risk. It is written in C++, which is not a part of our stack or expertise, so forking and maintaining was also not viable.
  2. Scaling and size limits. SSDB is not a distributed system and can only run on a single node. This imposes significant future scaling challenges, including at one point forcing us to cap blob sizes at 1 MB because latency degrades on larger payloads.

As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were:

  • A key-value blob store with a simple API.
  • Designed for multi-megabyte blob read/write ops and high throughput. We sustain loads of thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second reading and writing arbitrary blobs. These are unpredictable and bursty thanks to the volatility in stock markets.
  • Horizontally scalable, distributed.
  • Disk-space efficiency / compression.
  • Easily maintainable and highly economical.

So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following:

  • We already run ScyllaDB for high-throughput workloads, but in our tests, it turned out to be suboptimal for large blobs. Significantly lower throughput and higher resource usage. We specifically want multi-megabyte blobs. Tombstones from frequent overwrites and TTL expiries require careful tuning in ScyllaDB.
  • We already have considerable experience with Postgres in our stack and experimented with storing blobs as columns, but it turned out to be severely suboptimal again for the use case in terms of performance and disk-space efficiency.
  • Has blob storage as one of the options, but is not primarily designed or optimized for it. Also, a large system with too many features.
  • Had the right primitives, but again, not architected for high throughput multi-MB blob writes.
  • Severe operational complexity and resource requirements. We didn’t even get to trying it out.
  • This was the closest candidate. However, there were a few blockers. Our use case is overwrite-heavy (a user changing their workspace) over the same key, and SeaweedFS keeps appending before compaction, which can cause disk usage to grow uncontrollably. Blobs have their own IDs, which then have to be mapped against user keys in a separate DB, adding another layer. It doesn’t support TTL per blob. Also, reasonably complex setup with many parts.
  • Object storage has high per-request latency for small blobs, high request costs under write-heavy workloads (writes are 50% of our traffic), and coarse lifecycle TTLs instead of exact key expiry. Not to mention, S3 would incur significant costs given thousands of ops per second and tens of millions of ops per day.
  • Raw filesystem (one file per blob): Putting blobs directly on disk meant implementing atomic writes and write batching, managing large numbers of files and directories, good old atomic read/write disk performance and inode headaches, and maintaining a separate metadata index for TTLs. Not to mention, orchestrating this over AWS storage volumes.

Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its 35% Faster Than The Filesystem claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates millions of tables every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens?

So we ended up building Blobasaur, an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB.

We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements:

  • Redis protocol compatibility (if possible at all): Every existing client already used standard Redis libraries (, , , , , ). If we could get a system that could be a drop-in replacement, that would allow us to leave existing services untouched and reduce risk significantly.
  • Low latency across payload sizes: It needed to serve both 2 KB settings blobs and 5 MB chart layouts with single-digit millisecond latency.
  • Built-in compression: Almost all our payloads are repetitive JSON, which compresses well.
  • Simple CRUD with TTLs: We didn’t need complex data structures, server-side scripting, or secondary queries. We just needed key-value and hash CRUD with key expiry.
  • Multi-node partitioning: We needed to split data across multiple machines so a single node wasn’t a bottleneck.
  • Relaxed durability is acceptable: This store holds non-critical UI and workspace preferences, and not critical financial data. If a sudden power loss drops recent writes, a user might lose a recent chart layout tweak, which is annoying, but it never affects trading. This was a good performance trade-off for our use case.

We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves:

  • Atomic writes and batching.
  • TTL cleanup, which needs secondary indexes or walking the directories.
  • Managing metadata separately from the raw data.

SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB.

Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc.

While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust (, , and ), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary.

Splitting data into shards

In WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly.

To get write concurrency on a single machine, Blobasaur splits data across multiple SQLite database files on disk, called shards:

  • Consistent hashing: Each key maps to one shard via multi-probe consistent hashing.
  • Per-shard writer with group commit: Each shard has a dedicated writer task fed by a bounded queue. Instead of committing one key at a time, the writer drains a batch of pending writes from the queue and executes them inside a single BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT transaction. This amortizes transaction and WAL overhead across concurrent clients.
  • Concurrent readers: Reads go directly to a per-shard pool of read-only SQLite connections and can run concurrently with the writer.

How much does sharding help?

We benchmarked 1 shard against 16 shards using a load generator opening 64 concurrent connections. Each request used a 64 KiB JSON blob payload (close to our production average), which zstd compresses roughly 9x.

All runs used 100,000 keys, synchronous writes, and , with the data directory on to isolate SQLite locking and CPU overhead from disk variance. Both setups received the same total resources: 1,600 MB of SQLite page cache and 64 total read connections.

14,227 ops/s, p99 10.5 ms

With 16 shards, write throughput increases 3.3x and median write latency drops from 8.2 ms to 2.1 ms. Read throughput stays nearly identical because SQLite WAL mode already serves concurrent readers without contention.

At 25,324 operations per second, each carrying a 64 KiB payload, Blobasaur processes roughly 1.66 GB/s of uncompressed JSON through zstd. Both the server and load generator ran on the same 16-core laptop, sharing its CPU resources.

Our services use both plain keys (/) and Redis hashes (/) to group blobs by service or feature (for example, ).

Inside each shard, plain keys live in a table:

writes to . writes to a table for its namespace, , with the same columns. For example, stores in .

Expiry is stored in on the same row. Read queries filter out expired rows at read time (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > ?), while a background worker reaps expired rows asynchronously. Because the index on is a partial index (WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL), rows without a TTL take up no space in the expiry index.

Blobasaur supports zstd, lz4, gzip, and brotli compression before writing to SQLite. We run zstd in production.

Here is the compression ratio across one hour of production traffic:

With SQLite’s default 4 KiB pages, shrinking a 63.6 KiB payload to 5.5 KiB reduces its storage footprint from roughly 16 pages to roughly 2, before accounting for row and index overhead. Fewer pages holding blob data means less pressure on the page cache and less data to write through the WAL and into the database.

Because we don’t require strict durability for our specific use case of UI preferences, shards run in WAL mode with PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL. SQLite does not fsync on every transaction commit. An OS crash or power loss can lose recent committed transactions that have not yet been synced to durable storage, while preserving database consistency.

For workloads that want even lower write latency, Blobasaur also supports an optional mode that acknowledges writes as soon as they enter the shard’s memory queue, before the SQLite batch commits.

To scale beyond a single server, Blobasaur implements the Redis Cluster protocol, making it compatible with standard cluster-aware Redis clients. Like Redis Cluster, the keyspace is divided into 16384 hash slots using . Each Blobasaur node owns a configured range of slots, and nodes discover each other via gossip. If a client sends a key to the wrong node, the node responds with a redirect pointing to the owner node.

This gives Blobasaur two-level routing:

  1. Cluster level: selects the machine.
  2. Node level: Multi-probe consistent hashing selects the SQLite shard on that machine.

There are some limitations right now. At present, slot assignment is static in config. Live slot rebalancing between running nodes and automatic failover are not implemented yet.

Changing the number of shards

We chose multi-probe consistent hashing so resharding a node only has to move minimal data, without needing virtual nodes. With naive , increasing from 4 to 5 shards moves ~80% of keys. With consistent hashing, only ~20% of keys move (the share belonging to the new shard).

Resharding is currently an offline operation via the built-in CLI:

  1. Run blobasaur shard migrate 4 5 --verify.
  2. Update in and start the server.

The migration tool moves keys whose target shard changed. With , it checks that keys are in the expected shards and reports post-migration row counts.

We rolled out Blobasaur in a phased deployment strategy:

  1. New workloads first: When we launched Kite Terminal mode, we pointed its workspace storage directly at Blobasaur.
  2. Dual-write and backfill: For existing workloads like chart preferences, we updated the services to dual-write to both SSDB and Blobasaur while running a background migration for historical keys. Reads went to Blobasaur first and fell back to SSDB on a cache miss or error.
  3. Cutover: On the client side, the only code change was switching from a single-node Redis client to a Redis Cluster client with the three Blobasaur node IPs.

After running dual-writes for a month with zero discrepancies, we turned off SSDB.

What we learned along the way

Deleting rows doesn’t shrink SQLite files

Early on, we noticed disk usage only grew, even after millions of keys expired or were deleted. By default, SQLite keeps freed pages on an internal freelist for future writes rather than returning space to the OS.

To fix this, we enabled PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL across every shard and added a subcommand to reclaim unused freelist pages within a set allocation (128 MB default). Since shrinking the actual database file in WAL mode requires a checkpoint, Blobasaur runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) right after executing an incremental vacuum.

Async writes have to be visible to every read

When is enabled, a write returns while still sitting in the shard’s memory queue waiting for the next batch commit. To preserve read-your-writes consistency, queued writes are also placed in an in-memory pending map that reads check before querying SQLite.

During testing, we hit edge cases where certain read and existence-check paths bypassed this pending map or didn’t account for deletes. For example, a followed immediately by a could return the old value from SQLite because the queued hadn’t committed yet. We fixed this by storing explicit tombstones in the pending map and routing every read (, , , ) through it first.

Expiry cleanup has to share the writer

In production, our p99 write latency normally sat below 5 ms, but we occasionally saw spikes to 30 to 50 ms.

We traced the spikes to the background TTL cleanup task. Initially, the cleanup worker opened its own write connection and ran a single large statement for all expired rows. That large contended with the shard’s main writer for SQLite’s single write lock, stalling normal client batches.

We fixed this in two ways: routing cleanup batches through the shard’s existing writer connection so they take turns cleanly with client writes, and bounding each pass with (1,000 rows by default). Since expired rows are already filtered out at read time, spreading physical deletion across smaller chunks eliminated the latency spikes without affecting correctness.

Our current Blobasaur deployment runs as a three-node (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) cluster. Over a full trading session (09:00 to 15:30), p99 latency across all commands stays around 2 ms on every node, and p50 sits between 250 and 550 µs.

Broken down by command, p99 sits around 2 ms, p99 around 1.4 ms, and p99 mostly under 1 ms.

Blobasaur is open source under the AGPLv3 license and available on GitHub @iamd3vil/blobasaur. Find other projects from the Zerodha.tech hacker collective at 4th Cross Labs.

items.title: 15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP
items.author: fessguid
items.content:
Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there aren’t enough web servers for everyone. Let’s run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldn’t get funding, so we’re bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, I’ll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and we’ll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.

Instead of vibe coding it all, let’s use an ancient technique called . First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.

  1. - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socket
  2. - syscall, accepts a connection on a socket
  3. - receives data from a socket

What is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Let’s use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with .

It couldn’t be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that we’ve learned everything, let’s finish the article and call it a day:

Hm, why did fail? Ah, we’ve run out of ports! We’re using , so the kernel picks an available port from .

Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.

  • Ports are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You don’t want to call and end up allocating port to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.
  • Ports are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.

Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using , but that’s still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Let’s simply connect new network cards to the server.

The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a , so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldn’t be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, we’ll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!

I’ve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didn’t get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Can’t we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?

Let’s use a beautiful technology called , which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. We’ll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:

And now we can finally finish the article.

Hm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would take… 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.

By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.

TLDR: We’re using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main process’s memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.

Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, we’re doomed to build another specialised runtime. Let’s get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?

Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. What’s the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Let’s take another look at the loop.

This code has only two state variables, and . Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, we’d need to save the following state:

We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. We’re playing it safe here - we don’t need the full or , and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?

Here’s what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.

  • 14M idle connections - 0 bytes
  • Scheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB
  • 1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GB

Only half of our RAM budget, yay! I don’t often exceed my own expectations. Let’s validate it:

Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. I’m not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, it’s too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - let’s dive into networking in the kernel.

Remember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:

That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Let’s ask AI where all the memory goes:

TCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeeping
A 128-byte with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and padding
Open-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socket
The sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeeping

Potato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some , but it doesn’t look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. It’s Sunday and I have few tokens left, so we’ll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?

What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we can’t solve a task, we’re working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hm… level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!

The OSI model is… um… something I studied at university. Yeah, that’s a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, that’s exactly what operating at the and layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?

Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.

TCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkels’s Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.

There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:

  • gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stack
  • Seastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDB
  • lwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IP

Go, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but they’re nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So we’ll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:

So, and call it a day? Not so fast. is essentially a smart parser and can’t do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:

  • is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layer
  • is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layer
  • lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernel

is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and they’re easy to use.

But what about the third option, ? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: it’s common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.

lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and you’re done; when you want to read what you’ve received - it’s already there.

There’s another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, , and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. lets you avoid all that, but there’s a cost.

works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:

There’s another, less obvious nuance. requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers can’t work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the driver for your network interface… it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in , if you enable it over SSH, you’ll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.

Actually, there’s a fourth option now - Linux now has an subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. supports an alternative mode, , which is even closer to : you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but is very close (and simply easier to manage).

To support and in , we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for to help us.

  1. The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memory
  2. The runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by one
  3. Guest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the network stack and its adapters
  4. All 15M guests start listening, each on its own address
  5. The scheduler polls for incoming data from adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the next

And now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With , RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with just behind it:

Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.

is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.

items.author: jdns
items.content:
Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital . Upcasing it writes two bytes, , but the loop only bounds-checks one ().

The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.

The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by , , and .

UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is () when upcasing or () when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length.

Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds.
