items.title: LLM assisted reverse engineering
items.author: ioma8
items.content:
I have been hacking both hardware and software for 2 decades. Previously manually. But in 2026 with the help of AIs the proccess is greatly sped up. Below I will describe my proccess briefly or how I do it.

Tools which I mostly use are these:

What I basically do nowadays is just point the agent at the binary to be analysed and use my set of dedicated agent skills. Rest usually takes care of itself. But putting the skills besides, the flow is basically this.

  1. Find binary type, platform, build etc - based on this using appropriate decompiler (note - current AIs do fairly well with just disassembly . ie pure x86 or ARM instructions).
  2. Command agent to document all findings along the way to MD files. This serves several purposes. They become notes for your own understanding. They help the agent not lose the track after compaction / handoff to different agent. And last but not least, it helps the agent work more effectively, not get lost in circles etc. More about this later.
  3. Ask the agent to analyse basic structure. Main functions, main branching, imported functions etc of given binary. By binary I mean whatever. Desktop executable, website or firmware image.

Once I have this basic overview I can usually proceed any way I need to do modifications to the original binary or build mods or just help me understand it better.

On some occasions some things are not easily resolvable by simple disassembly or decompilation. In those cases you can do:

  • Let the agent debug given binary and set breakpoints on specific parts to help it figure out given inner workings.
  • Use logging. Either by somehow enabling it in the original binary or by making a probe (and this can mean many things) that injects to the original binary and records you via logs (to file) whatever is needed to resolve given feature.
  • Give agent outside access - ie computer use for desktop apps, or api controllable emulator for running and controlling given firmware.
  • Ask agent to try different approach. But you must be specific. Ie when it gets stuck in disasembly by following xrefs, ask it to try to follow strings in the binary instead.
  • Read the entire LLM conversation and thinking. Current LLMs are smart but they still sometimes get to a narrow approach. By reading the traces you can often instinctively figure the agent it going into a blind path and give it suggestion as to how it might be approached better. That however skill of your own to have.

Here are some of my major skills I use frequently.

It gives you several questions when your input might be valuable. I usually use it with this prompt:

It helps a ton to have a skill where your specific reverse engineering tooling is described. Ie to use radare2 or kuna. Or description of how to use the MCP Ghidra bridge and for what. Without such a skill, agents often give up too quickly getting lost, not knowing how to do the actual disassembly / decompilation.

That is also my own skill. Its related to how I wrote earlier how important it is to make the agent document everything into MD files. This skill forces agent who is getting stuck to follow this loop:

  1. Make a hypothesis of why / how something works. Write it down into CSV table of hypotheses, saved on disc.
  2. Design experiment (probe, logging, ...) which will definitively prove or disprove this hypothesis.

This is variation of scientific method and it significantly helps agents when they are getting stuck on some problem. Stops it going in circles. By forcing it to do definitive experiments. No endless guessing and trying random things. This one is crucial in my opinion. I made it public too, so other can benefit from it.

Implementation of hacks and probes

For implementing anything I basically go for 2 toolings.

  1. Python but with UV tooling. UV tooling allows to make custom super quickly and portably. Also allows to make single-file, inline dependencies scripts. Python is great for prototyping or quickly making probes or even decompilation helpers.
  2. Rust for actual implementation of given hack. Whenever it is possible I am using rust for this. It has many reasons but he two main are:
  • it is very elegant language for me personally to work with and
  • it provides brutally good feedback loops to the agent when it iterates - the compiler is very strict and points the agent immediately to any possible memory or syntax issues he might be heading to. Of course rust has also its downsides, like slower compile times, but overal its mature language with plethora of build targets (I have implemented in it webs, desktop apps, hacks / trainers but even firmwares for various embedded languages).

With the AI assisted reverse engineering I was able to achieve such crazy reverse engineering succeses, in the last 6 months, which would take me years each on its own, if done by hands.

  • Completely mapped communication protocols of many devices like EmWave biofeedback device or both my Sony Alpha mirrorless cameras. Allowing me to make custom desktop and mobile apps for file transfer, wireless control and more. I even managed to make this way a wireless webcam from my A7III mirrorless camera.
  • Cracked tons of license-locked abandonware softwares from my youth
  • Developed custom lightweight Evernote client

Sometimes its a thin boundary between reverse engineering and software development. Sometimes you just decipher the proprietary save file format of the ugly paid app and then move into the clean software development phase of building your new, totally unique editor, to work with these files. (yes I made custom Photoshop too and its not the ArtCraft suite - I did it about a year before them, just for me).

Reverse engineering and hacking into old softwares or devices has always been a hobby for me. I understand assembly, I understand hardware. But it was long and tedious process.

With the cheap accesibility to smart LLM tools in these days, this hobby took dramatic turn for me. I do not miss manually analyzing the assembly instructions. But I love quickly getting the results. Yes my long experience helps me steer the agents the correct way. But that is also fun. And I am learning a ton of things along the way.

I wish everyone would try to do some hacks of his own. For me the hobby is driven by curiosity. And LLMs didn't take that away. They gave me turbo boost to my wonderings and explorations. Let's free our minds!

Edit: We are getting popular on HN! Didnt expect this one day after deploying my blog! Super happy!

items.title: Gemini 4 Neon
items.author: yigitdemirag
items.content:
Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work

Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index, it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench.

Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI, ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.

items.title: DaisyRose-27B
items.author: de_sty
items.content:
Today we are releasing , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning usingMiles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

We are releasing andcheckpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes.

High-quality Training Data

We built the tasks in partnership withEigent AI, starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 of them made it into the final training set. The training tasks are selected based on three criteria.

  • Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran the original Qwen3.8-27B on every training task and carefully redesigned each one so that it brings out the mistakes we want the model to stop making. We then tuned each task until its solve rate fell within a suitable range, neither too easy nor too hard for the model to learn from.
  • Every task is a long job with several problems chained together.Each task entails a chain of interdependent problems, so an agent has to navigate through multiple stages of reasoning, planning, and execution. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in the sandbox, with more than 100 tool-calls and more than 256k output tokens.
  • There is no room for reward hacking. We reviewed every task along with the model's attempts at it. Any task that could be passed without really solving it, or that had a design flaw, was fixed or removed before training.

Efficient training backend

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

On this release, 37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-sourceAgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time.

The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory.

Our cloud infrastructure cost for the project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes.

Try DaisyRose-27B, or train your own

You can download DaisyRose-27B fromHugging Face, and you can train your own agents with our open source reinforcement learning frameworkMiles.

DaisyRose-27B is one example of what high-quality data and efficient infrastructure can make possible. We are bringing this approach to teams building specialized models, with a focus on improving the capabilities they need while preserving the model’s broader strengths. If you are exploring post-training for your own model, reach out atcontact@radixark.ai.

We are deeply grateful to Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and to the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B, the foundation of our work. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, as well as other open-source projects, including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

  1. How we evaluated: Terminal Bench 4.1 is averaged over 8 runs per task, using our internal mini-swe-agent harness with summarization turned on. Terminal Bench 2.1 is averaged over 5 runs per task, using the Terminus 2 harness. DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE Bench Pro v2 are averaged over 8 and 5 runs per task, both using the mini-swe-agent harness. HLE (text-only) is averaged over 5 runs per problem, graded by GPT-6 Luna, with no tools. IFBench is averaged over 4 runs on each of its 300 prompts, scored by the official allenai/IFBench scorer as prompt-level loose accuracy on the final response, with the thinking left out. GPQA Diamond is averaged over 8 runs on each of its 198 questions, using the simple-evals multiple-choice template and answer extraction, with the answer order reshuffled on every run.↩

items.title: Genie 4 is now available
items.author: leumon
items.content:
The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism.

Beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix.

Learn how we are building responsibly

We are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings.

Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. For a deeper look into model limitations and our progress on these fronts, read our Genie 4 model research overview.

items.title: The Magic of Partial Evaluation
items.author: aray07
items.content:
There are certain ideas in software that are simply beautiful. It doesn't matter if they have any practical use. It doesn't matter that you will never convince your coworkers to consider them. There is just something captivating about the way some computational systems work.

For me, the most beautiful pieces of software are those that reveal something about the nature of programming languages. Programming languages are my obsession. I have never met a problem that couldn't be solved by introducing yet another programming language. Solving a problem at the programming language level is about solving the meta problem. Instead of trying to solve a particular problem, we take a step back and ask how we can solve a whole class of problems at once.

So when I find something that makes me rethink the nature of programming languages, I start rethinking computation as a whole. One of these incredibly beautiful but tricky concepts goes by the name partial evaluation. If you are fascinated by interpreters and compilers, partial evaluation will teach you how they are related, and how you can get a compiler for free.

Partial Evaluation Easy Mode#

Partial evaluation has been a fascination of mine for a while. But this whole thing came up when James Long announced he had revived Meta's partial evaluator for JavaScript called prepack. When I first heard about prepack, I had some high hopes and expectations for the project, but was sadly let down. This revival brought to light those same dreams. But sadly, just as with the original aim, prepack was not designed for beauty, but for practicality. So I figured it was time to renew my own efforts.

Yes, in some ways this is a post repping my own library I'm releasing. But I'm not doing this because I want it to be used. I'm doing this because it lets you play with the idea I find so beautiful. That is what this post is about.

Doing Partial Evaluation by Hand#

Consider the following code:

n  n n

As a person who reads code, you can think about how this code computes and what answer it will give. But you can do more than just give the answer. You can see the expanded form of this particular code for these particular calls. This code is spiritually the same as the following expression, once we expand it out.

In this case, there is really nothing at all that this code needs to do at runtime. A sufficiently smart compiler will just run this code directly at compile time and give the answer. But this is a bit less clear if things come in at runtime.

exponent  base base exponent processargv

It might seem like we can't do anything here, but again, if you are used to thinking about how programs run, you can trace this out and realize this is just the same as:

processargvprocessargvprocessargvprocessargvprocessargv

What we have done in both of these cases is called partial evaluation. In the first, it was a trivial case because everything was statically known. But in this latter case, we have reduced a program down into the essentials of its dynamic structure. There are no recursive function calls left. All of this has been expanded as far as it could till we get just the dynamic parts of the code remaining.

This intuitive notion of partial evaluation is all you need to know to appreciate the beauty here. Partial evaluation just evaluates the part of the program we can evaluate at build time and leaves all the rest. When we do this with certain programs in certain combinations, we get some quite surprising, incredible behavior.

 expr  exprexprexprexprexprexprexprexprexprexpr

Here we have a very simple interpreter for a language that just supports arithmetic. For the above expression, you should be able to think about how we could start "partially" evaluating it. (In this case, it can be a full evaluation.) If this kind of partial evaluation isn't quite clicking for you, I've put the steps below to hopefully help it make sense.


→ 
→ 
→ 
→ 
→ 
→ 
→

This is a simple evaluation of the code. But what happens if we throw a value we don't know into the expression?

processargv
→ processargv
→ processargv
→ processargv
→ processargv
→ processargv
→ processargv

Here we can see that clear partial evaluation difference. We don't know how to evaluate . We have no idea what the answer to that will be. But as part of this process, we do know some partial information about it. For example, when we get to

 expr  expr

we know that is indeed a number. So we can partially evaluate it further. Hopefully this is all making sense. But if you are like me, this all might seem a bit trivial and uninteresting. So let's look at a more complicated example.

code input  tape  jumps  stack  pointer  inputPointer  output  i  i  codelength icodei stackicodei start  stack
      jumpsstart i
      jumpsi start i  i  codelength icodei pointer pointer tapepointer tapepointer output  Stringtapepointer
        tapepointer inputPointer  inputlength
           inputinputPointertapepointer i  jumpsitapepointer i  jumpsi output

Here we have a brainfuck interpreter. And the example program we want to partially evaluate does not require any input at all (in brainfuck is the way you get input). So when we go to partially evaluate this, we will just get an answer. In this case, this program is actually brainfuck's "hello world". But what about a program with input?

 processargv

When we do our partial evaluation, we get the following:

 a
  a
    a  processargv
    a  a  a alength
      a  a a
    a 
  a a  Stringa

What is this? A compiled brainfuck program! This is the first incredible fact: when you take an interpreter and partially evaluate it with a program, you get the compiled program out! Now this particular exact form is an artifact of how my partial evaluator works. You could imagine slightly different code. But the key is that what we've done is remove the interpreter completely.

What we've discovered here is the first of three so-called Futamura Projections. Our partial evaluator, when applied to an interpreter and given a program, can give us a compiled version of that program. Or to put it in pseudocode.

partial_eval(interpreter, prog) -> compiled_prog

Depending on your exposure to interpreters and compilers, this might seem miraculous or mundane. Writing an interpreter and writing a compiler can seem like significantly different undertakings. In the age of AI, perhaps less so, but I think even then many things still hold. It is quite easy to instrument an interpreter, quite a bit harder to do so for a compiler. Changing an interpreter to support new features is quite easy, less so for a compiler. But more than that, there are all sorts of things that can be thought of as interpreters, that we'd almost never write a compiler for.

schematype value schemaminLength  valuelength  schemaminLength value  Numbervalueschemamin  value  schemamin value Arrayvalue length  valuelength i  i  length ii  value schemaitems valuei value  value Arrayvalue
        Objectschemaproperties
          Objectvalue keyschemapropertieskey valuekey schematype userSchema 
  type
  properties
    name type minLength
    age type min
    tags type items typeuserSchema value

Consider this simple schema setup. This is code that can easily be partially evaled into something where we have created specialized functions for our particular schema. While not the most crucial code, this can give us a 5x performance boost when our objects start getting more complicated. You may think that we should just hand-write those functions. Or hand-write a compiler for these schemas. But what about those schemas that exist only at runtime? Now we either need to compile those on the fly, or we have to keep both a compiler and interpreter. Having a way to partial eval lowers this burden quite a bit.

But if the Futamura projections stopped here, they would be exciting, but not quite the craziness they are. To understand how this can go further, we are going to take this a step beyond your raw intuition of what it means to partially evaluate something and give a different frame. We can think of partial evaluation as a process of "specializing" a program.

What exactly is specializing a program? Well, it is taking a program that is generic and making a version that instead works for a single program. Let's think about a simple pattern matcher program like an overly simplified regex.

patternlength  textlength  firstCharacterMatches 
    textlength  pattern text allowsRepetition  patternallowsRepetition remainingPattern  patternremainingPattern textfirstCharacterMatches remainingText  textpattern remainingTextfirstCharacterMatches remainingPattern  pattern remainingText  textremainingPattern remainingText

This program is generic. It lets you match on many different patterns. That can be great if we need that flexibility. But if you don't have a bunch of patterns, it might be worth it to just make specialized code. Now, exactly what kind of specialized code? It might be that you only have this literal pattern; then you want to specialize very particularly.

 i texti itexti i texti i  textlength

Or you just have as a pattern.

 i i  textlength  texti x ii  textlength  texti y ii  textlength  texti z i i  textlength

For any bit of generic code, we can think of how to move our code to a more specialized form.

Specializing the Specializer#

Partial evaluation is a form of specialization that figures out what it should specialize on based on what input is static and what is dynamic. In many ways, a partial evaluator is a generic specializer. Given any program, we can make a specialized version of it for any input. What happens if we specialize an interpreter for a given input? We get back that interpreter for only exactly that one program. But what do we need then? Do we need all this generic dispatch? No, we know the full program. We don't need any operations we don't actually use. We can fully get rid of all the generic interpreter mechanism.

But if the specializer can specialize any program, can it specialize itself?

This leads us to the second Futamura projection. Put in our pseudo-code format, we get:

partial_eval(partial_eval, interpreter) -> compiler

Or, to put it in our specializer language, what if we make a special version of our generic specializer? What is it specialized for? A particular interpreter. Now we have a function that, given any program, will spit out newly specialized interpreters just for that program. Or, in Java speak, we have a specialized interpreter factory.

Let's see a real example of one of these compilers to make this concrete. Here is the interpreter we are going to specialize.

 value programlength  instruction  programinstruction 
      value  ioinstruction 
      iovalue instruction

    program  program value

When we apply our second projection, we get out the following compiler:

 lines  codegen literalSource  codegensource remaining  program value  literalSourceremaininglength  remainingItem  remainingremainingItem  ioReference  codegen callSource lines ioReferencesource
      remaining  remaining
      value  callSourceremainingItem  ioReference2  codegen args codegenvaluelines ioReference2 args
      remaining  remaining text  remainingItemtext valueReference  codegenvalue codegenlines valueReference

And if we compile one of these very simple programs, we can see the output:

 v0  io v1  iov0 v0

Now, of course, this is not a very interesting language. But hopefully you can see this general idea. Given an interpreter, we automatically derive a compiler! Pretty incredible.

But we can't stop at the second projection. We have to push on and get to the final mind-bending projection. If you apply our specializer to itself as input, you get a compiler generator.

partial_eval partial_eval compiler_generator

So now we have a generic function that will spit out compilers for any interpreter we give it!

I have implemented a reasonable, but still very limited partial evaluator for JavaScript in Rust. I have taken it further to try to make it work quite well for a number of different interpreters and interpreter-like programs in JavaScript. I've also tried to get limited versions of the second and third projections working. Go play with it, see what works, what doesn't, file issues, or better, use some of your tokens to help me make more cases work.

But most of all, explore. This is such a rich space. Below are some papers, blogs, and projects about partial evaluation in some way, shape, or form. There has never been a better time to play with these kinds of crazy techniques for programming languages. Don't let what is practical stop you from exploring the cool, interesting aspects of programming.

items.title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
items.author: codekarate
items.content:
Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi.

Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races.

Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself.

At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans.

There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack.

Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc).

When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI.

We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead.

You can get started with `npm create factory`.

It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!

items.title: AI agents ask better questions than KPMG accountants in audit trial
items.author: Betelbuddy
items.content:
LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team.

The experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an important development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how quickly will the economics of auditing change?

According to the , the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions.

Join The European Business Briefing

New subscribers this quarter are entered into a draw to win a Rolex Submariner. Join 40,000+ founders, investors and executives who read EBM every day.

Subscribe

KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into issues than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised.

The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged.

From supporting accountants to conducting audits

Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow.

The agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation.

The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the company’s accounts.

Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks.

KPMG plans to expand the initiative to as many as 20 larger audits, although the firm acknowledges that the technology is not yet sufficiently mature to be deployed across thousands of engagements. Data quality also remains a significant obstacle, with some businesses lacking the clean, structured information required for AI agents to operate effectively.

A challenge to the Big Four business model?

The implications for the accountancy industry could be substantial.

Traditional auditing relies on large teams of junior accountants undertaking detailed and repetitive work, supervised by experienced managers and partners. AI agents potentially offer a different operating model, automating significant portions of data collection, analysis and documentation while allowing senior professionals to concentrate on complex judgements and exceptions.

For firms such as KPMG, Deloitte, PwC and EY, the attraction is clear: faster audits, potentially lower operating costs and the ability to analyse much larger volumes of financial information.

However, whether those savings will ultimately be passed on to clients remains uncertain. KPMG has acknowledged the potential for significant time savings but has not confirmed whether AI-driven efficiencies will translate into lower audit fees.

Human judgement remains the final safeguard

The transition also presents regulatory and professional challenges. The UK’s Financial Reporting Council has warned that the use of AI must not undermine auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism.

There are also concerns about data security, over-reliance on automated conclusions and the possibility of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. The fundamental responsibility for an audit opinion remains with the human auditor, regardless of the technology used.

The KPMG experiment does not establish that AI can replace accountants or independently deliver a reliable statutory audit. It does, however, demonstrate that AI agents are beginning to challenge professionals in areas that were once considered dependent on human expertise.

For the accountancy profession, the question is no longer simply whether AI will become part of the audit process. It is how much of that process will eventually be performed by machines — and what role human accountants will play when it does.

items.title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
items.author: speedping
items.content:
• Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.

  • Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

  • The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.

  • We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.

  • We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.

  • Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.

  • F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.

  • : Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.

  • : F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.

  • F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered  CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.Wiz Atlas, the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.

The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the

PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.

Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.

In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.

NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.

On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.

The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module.

An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs.

We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes.

F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table): 

Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances:

Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading.

Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities.

CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable

NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.

We start by sending only part of a frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams,ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest:

ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1);

if (h2c->state.incomplete) {

When we send the rest of the frame,ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments . However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close.

Triggering the use-after-free

Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.

Opening an upstream connection calls When free connection slots run low, selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.

Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free.

From use-after-free to remote code execution

The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection.

This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow

Returning credit for unsent data

HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called .

When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:

h2c->send_window += window;

This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur.

A bounds check that no longer works

The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update(), which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:

if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window)

The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases.

From an invalid length to remote code execution

The invalid counter eventually reaches , where it is converted to the signed integer type to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer.

When the TLS send path in processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module.

To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.

Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets.

Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation.

Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.

As we saw with PHP2Shell, AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve.

The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it.

Hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.
